MR. HERRIDGE-USE IN COMMITTEE OF DOCUMENT NOT TABLED IN HOUSE
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege is that certain documents were improperly made available to the hon. member for Kootenay East by a senior official of the Department of External Affairs before those documents had been tabled in the house. This action was taken during a meeting of the external affairs committee held yesterday afternoon, and in my opinion it constituted an offence against the rules of the house and a grave discourtesy to its members.
On Wednesday, May 6 I moved the following motion:
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all petitions sponsored by the Nelson chamber of commerce signed by residents of Kootenay East and West urging immediate ratification of the Columbia river treaty, received by the government since January 1, 1964.
This motion was unanimously agreed to. During the meeting of the external affairs committee yesterday afternoon a senior official of the Department of External Affairs, at two minutes after 5 p.m., handed the hon. member for Kootenay East the original petition referred to in my motion. I wish to bring Your Honour's attention to the fact that the hon. member for Kootenay East is not at present a member of the government. Shortly afterward the hon. member for Kootenay East commenced to use this document as evidence before the committee.
At that point I immediately rose on a question of privilege to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that the document was improperly before the committee. The hon. member for Leeds, the esteemed chairman of the committee, then suggested I be permitted to see the petition. However, out of respect for the rules of this house and the rights of members of parliament I refused to look at the document until it came into my hands legally in accordance with the rules of the house.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully suggest that the members of this house are entitled to an explanation of the reasons for this unusual breach of the rules of this house, and are entitled to an apology from the member for Kootenay East and the senior official of the Department of External Affairs involved in this breach of the rules and grave discourtesy to the members of this house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MR. HERRIDGE-USE IN COMMITTEE OF DOCUMENT NOT TABLED IN HOUSE
speechtext:
I might have risen and suggested that raising this particular question of privilege seems to me out of order at this time. The question has to do with a matter which is before a committee that is sitting, and the place to raise such a question of privilege is, I believe, in that committee. However, I am not rising to make a technical objection, except to remind my esteemed and sensitive friend of what I believe to be the correct procedure.
I am sure we would all regret it, if the hon. gentleman has been unfairly dealt with. The fact is that his question concerns a petition containing some 4,000 or 5,000 names of people from the hon. gentleman's constituency who are urging the government to get on with the Columbia river treaty. I referred to this petition when I was speaking in the house on the question of the Columbia river treaty.
Yesterday, or the day before yesterday, the hon. gentleman had on the order paper a motion which was accepted by the house asking for the production of this document. It takes time to provide several copies of it, and the hon. member for Kootenay East asked one of the officials of the Department of External Affairs if he might see the petition. The official, who is one of the responsible officials of the department, as the hon. gentleman knows, thought there was no reason why this should not be permitted. If the hon. member for Kootenay West had asked for it he would have obtained it. However, with these facts in mind I am looking into the matter further to try to deal with the situation in a manner which, I know, will end in the full satisfaction of the sensitive nature of my esteemed and dear friend the hon. member for Kootenay West.

subtopic: MR. HERRIDGE-USE IN COMMITTEE OF DOCUMENT NOT TABLED IN HOUSE
speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which not only affects me personally but I think affects many hon. members of the house. I realize and appreciate that the rules say I should raise a question of privilege as soon as possible. My question of privilege arises out of a comment made yesterday in reference to the report brought in by the rules committee. The comment was made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). I was unable to hear it at the time because of the noise from that particular party following the remarks I made. The words I refer to are these:
As long as we have a democracy in this country I think the hon. member for Bow River will have to abide by the decision of the electorate.
Either the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam deliberately misinterpreted what I said or he unintentionally misinterpreted it, because I was not speaking against splinter parties as such or against the situation with regard to those constituencies which may elect members of splinter parties; I was saying there has grown up in this house a procedure, now endorsed by the rules committee, of giving a spokesman for each of those parties an opportunity to make comments in reply to statements on government policies made from the treasury benches from time to time. Here we are in the process of amending our rules because we wish to save time in the house, and we now have five parties in the opposition. I only said that in the future we may have 10 or 20.

maintopic: MR. WOOLLIAMS    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR BURNABY-COQUITLAM
speechtext: Well, four parties in the opposition; you are absolutely correct. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam deliberately misinterpreted my statement because he was frightened that the Canadian people would find out the truth and import of my remarks.

[Mr. Speaker.!

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture arising out of several reports that there have been some significant recent sales of butter or butter oil out of government surplus stock. speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: BUTTER OIL
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ADDITIONAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure it will be a matter of interest to all members of the house to know that progress has been made in the sale of the agricultural stabilization board surplus holdings of butter oil. The board, in its oil program, converted some 105 million pounds of butter into approximately 85 million pounds of butter oil. This was offered for export sale at 27 cents a pound to approved markets on November 1, 1963. From that date to the present some 20 million pounds had been sold on export markets.
I am pleased to announce that the board has now completed sales agreements with 11 Canadian firms for the disposal of an additional 50 million pounds on export markets. The bulk of these shipments are expected to be made during the next three or four months. While it is not considered to be in the best interests of the firms involved to disclose the
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1

terms and conditions of these contracts, all contracts involve a forfeitable performance deposit. Thus, in essence, the government's entire stock of butter oil, other than that which is considered necessary to service the domestic market, is at present committed for sale. This leaves the board with total butter and butter oil stocks of approximately 90 million pounds.
Obviously our butter situation is considerably improved from what it has been in the last few years. However, it would be premature to suggest that we have yet arrived at any permanent solution to the problems of the dairy industry. I think the experience of the dairy industry over the last few years indicates that some further adjustments will eventually have to be made in dairy programs if we are to arrive at a solution to the industry's problems. I do not want to suggest in any way that I think our producers are getting more help from the government than they deserve, but we do not want any of our programs to encourage conditions that just do not make economic sense.

He said: Mr. Speaker, as set out on the order paper, the purpose of this resolution is to appoint a special committee on defence to continue the work started by a similar committee in the past session.
The house will recall that the resolution appointing the original committee was proposed by the Prime Minister on May 30, and the motion was agreed to by the house on June 7. The committee began its hearings on June 18, and by the time the interim report was tabled in the house a total of 45 meetings were held including 29 in Canada, two in the United States and 14 in Europe. In addition to travelling abroad the committee set a number of precedents, including hearing from senior service officers and individuals outside the government. The committee also received expert military and political advice here in Canada, in the United States and in Europe.
Personally I feel that the committee performed a very useful function. The members from all parties pursued their assignment in a very responsible manner in devoting themselves to the very complex problems of defence. Not only were the members of the committee made aware of the problems facing defence, but also members of the press and through them the public.
I might say that the government found the recommendations of the committee of great assistance and I think it was very rewarding, in a parliament of minorities, to have the members of the committee on defence adopt a non-partisan approach to their work. Certainly one result of this was that the calibre of the debate when the estimates of the Department of National Defence came before parliament in 1963 was of a much higher order than in previous years, due to the contribution made to the debate by individual members of the committee representing all political parties in the house.
The government has every confidence that the reconstitution of the committee called for

in this resolution will serve a very useful purpose, and I am hopeful that upon adoption of this motion the committee can begin its sittings very shortly.
I have already said that it is the intention of the government to refer the amendment to the National Defence Act, which we are to discuss later today, to the committee after completion of second reading. I understand, Mr. Speaker, that there is agreement to approve this motion, that we will have a general debate on defence on second reading of the bill to amend the National Defence Act, and that the debate on that bill will not be restricted to its immediate terms but will be allowed to cover the whole field of defence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill C-90, to amend the National Defence Act.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to implement one of the major recommendations included in the white paper on defence. Specifically, the bill provides for the replacement of the present positions of chairman of the chiefs of staff committee, chief of the naval staff, chief of the general staff and chief of the air staff by a single new position designated as chief of the defence staff. This change is the first and perhaps the most important move in the integration of the armed forces under a single defence staff.
At this point I should like to express my appreciation of the support given to this proposal by the Prime Minister and the government of Canada. The enthusiastic response has been most gratifying and is deeply appreciated. I should like in particular to thank my colleague the associate minister for his untiring assistance. In carrying, as he does, the main burden of the administrative load in the department he has contributed immeasurably to the work we have jointly undertaken. Without this support any major reorganization on the scale contemplated would not be possible.
The establishment of a single chief of defence staff will permit the reorganization of our armed forces on a functional basis. This will not only simplify procedures and permit the development of a more efficient fighting force, but it will also greatly facilitate the implementation of a long range, co-ordinated defence policy as set out in the white paper. In the absence of a unified defence staff the implementation of such a policy would be extremely difficult and, in my opinion, virtually impossible.
In considering the organization of the armed forces a number of options were studied. These included the status quo, the Glassco commission recommendations and the decision which was finally adopted, that is to say the complete integration of the forces commencing at the top with the integration of the command structure.
First in respect to the status quo, may I say there are at the present time six routes of information coming to the minister. Direct access is afforded to the chairman of the chiefs of staff on behalf of the chiefs of staff committee; to the chief of the naval staff, to the chief of the general staff, to the chief

National Defence Act
of the air staff, to the chief of the defence research board and to the deputy minister. The minister is inadequately staffed to coordinate at his level and in his office the information coming from these several sources. Projects are not always co-ordinated into a single plan. It is in effect, in its present application, a system which is virtually unmanageable, and the minister is unable to exercise his constitutional authority adequately.
In considering alternatives which would permit the minister to exercise his responsibility effectively, the recommendation of the Glassco commission was considered. In essence the suggestion was that a number of support functions be transferred from the individual services to the chairman of the chiefs of staff for administration. This suggestion was given careful consideration because it is in line with procedures in other countries, and has long been put forward as a course which might be adopted in this country.
However, we came to the conclusion that this proposal would not likely result in a real reduction of manpower. On the contrary, it seemed to us it would probably result in a continuation and perhaps even an amplification of the committee system. If the chairman were given power to impose decisions made in these various areas on the individual services, then the real power of the individual chiefs of staff would be substantially diminished. If, on the other hand, he was not given power to impose decisions in those areas and the acceptance of his proposals depended on persuasion and the accommodation of views, then the committee system with all its inevitable delays and frustrations would remain. Based on experience both in Canada up to the present time and in other countries we came to the conclusion that this would not meet the two real needs as we see them; first of all a more effective organization and, second, a considerable reduction in duplication in headquarters.
The third alternative, which was the one finally adopted, was the integration of the armed forces into a single unit. This was decided on because it was considered to be the only solution likely to achieve those two important objectives (a) a more streamlined and effective system, and (b) reduced manpower due to reduction in duplications and increased efficiency in headquarters, command, training, logistics and support organizations.
At this point I should like to emphasize that I have no criticism of the men who

have served their country in senior military positions. On the contrary, they have served Canada and the military organizations of which they were and are a part with courage, devotion and distinction. Man for man there are no better armed forces than ours, and we are proud of the men and women who serve us so well. The organization of our available forces can, however, be improved so as to provide greater effectiveness, and in this area responsibility for taking the initiative lies with the minister and the government. The constitutional authority and responsibility is clear, and if changes in organization are required it is the responsibility of the government to recommend them and to see that they are implemented. We have placed our recommendations before parliament and now seek the statutory amendments necessary to get on with the job. We have the backing of the great majority of the Canadian people, and the enthusiastic support of the men and women of the armed forces.
As I indicated, we believe that the proposed new organization will result not only in a more efficient and responsive service but that it will also permit substantial reductions in manpower in headquarters, training and other units. It is, of course, impossible to predict the exact extent of the savings because there is no experience on which to base our estimates. For the purposes of planning, however, we have guessed that it will be possible to reduce service requirements by approximately 10,000 without affecting our operational elements.

speechtext: Over all?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Over all. This estimate predicts a 20 per cent average saving in the
50,000	personnel employed in headquarters, regional headquarters, training and other support units. Of these we believe the largest saving can be effected at national defence headquarters. If we reach our goal we expect that the saving in dollars will amount to approximately $100 million annually, or $1 billion over a ten year period.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question? I wonder if he is not incorrect in talking about a saving. The impression has got abroad that he is going to save $100 million from total expenditure, but all he is doing is transferring a certain reduction in one area to expenditure in another area.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I should be glad to clear up that point. First, we have saved $100 million and the defence estimates have been reduced

by that amount as compared with previous years. So there is a saving to the taxpayers of approximately that amount. There is, in addition to that, a $100 million a year saving which we are now talking about, which is a diversion from overhead costs to military equipment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Then let us not call it a saving.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: This is a saving in the overhead establishment which should be available to be diverted for the acquisition of new equipment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Let us say "reduction".

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: If there is some word which would please my hon. friends more, I would be happy to use it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: By saying "saving" you are confusing the public.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This reduction, or saving, will assist us in the difficult task of getting our defence expenditures back in balance. We must increase the proportion of funds available for new equipment if we are to have a viable and effective force in the years to come. The present proportion of about 14 per cent for equipment is unacceptably low and must be increased to something of the order of 25 per cent in the years ahead. Even this proportion is not high compared to other forces. The additional moneys available for equipment will not only permit us to keep our forces in better fighting shape; it will also have a beneficial effect on our Canadian defence industries. The advantage of a long range plan will permit them to plan more effectively and to assist us in meeting our equipment needs. Peaks and valleys of production will be evened out to the maximum extent possible, and the commercial and export aspects of defence requirements will be kept in mind in our planning.
I would like to say a word about the effects of the proposed reorganization on service personnel. First of all, as announced by the Associate Minister of National Defence this morning, we plan special benefits for those who will be retired in advance of their normal retirement age. This will be done as integration proceeds and as reductions occur in many branches of the armed forces, particularly in the support units. This will result in the necessity to retire some personnel. There is no question as to the loyalty, efficiency and faithful service of those who will be affected, but officers and men
National Defence Act
selected for premature retirement will be those for whom appropriate employment cannot be found within the reorganized defence force. Established positions will be eliminated when the functions now carried out by two or more individuals are amalgamated into one.
The government appreciates that the termination of service of an officer or man, through no fault of his own, may place him in a position of undue hardship. In recognition of this a special cash benefit will be provided to assist him to rehabilitate himself in civilian employment. The special gratuity is partial compensation for the loss of anticipated future earnings and reduced pension benefits. This special cash payment, which is subject to income tax, will be in addition to any normal leave or pension entitlement. The benefit will not apply to those who are released for reasons of misconduct or inefficiency, or who request their release.
The amount of the special cash benefit, to be paid in one lump sum, will increase with length of service up to a maximum of the equivalent of 10 months pay for those with 15J or more years of service. It will be reduced progressively as normal retirement age is approached. Officers serving on short service commissions are in a special category. The period of time by which their service is shortened will be the basis for calculating their benefits.
In addition to this special cash gratuity, the government will propose to parliament that the present provision in the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act which provides a 5 per cent reduction in annuities for servicemen who have less than 20 years service but more than 10 years service be waived. This will be accomplished by the inclusion of an item in the next supplementary estimates of the Department of National Defence to obtain statutory authority for treasury board to direct payment of a full, immediate annuity to contributors under the act.
In so far as those who will continue to be required, Mr. Speaker-and this includes most of those now serving-there will be excellent career opportunities. I am confident that the reorganization of the Canadian armed forces will lead to greater opportunities for many of those who are now serving and for those entering the service now and in the future.
The main purpose of our program is to achieve a better balance between the combat forces and the supporting elements, and to streamline and modernize the management system. In the process there will be a reduction in over-all numbers. There will not, however, be any reduction of effectiveness

National Defence Act
and efficiency, or any elimination of positions that contribute to the capability of the forces to perform their assigned roles.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, it will be necessary for us to continue to recruit new men. I think this is most important. The services have a continuing need for young men. Our armed forces are very much living organizations and require a constant infusion of new blood to keep them in prime condition. For those with ability and determination, the armed forces offer expanded career prospects and opportunities in the service of Canada and the cause of world peace. Therefore I urge hon. members to encourage young men to volunteer to serve their country in the armed forces.
While the amendments to the legislation before the house are not concerned with the civil aspects of the department, I wish to say something about the important subject of civilian control. As we stated in the white paper on defence, the responsibility of the minister to maintain an effective civilian control raises, in the words of the royal commission on government organization, "a need for a strong staff group which is essentially civilian in character, outside the framework of the armed forces". This civilian staff group is supplied through the deputy minister and his permanent staff. There is no need to change the legislation relating to the deputy minister. The National Defence Act now provides, under section 7, for the appointment of a deputy minister. As in the case of deputy ministers of other departments, this position is defined under the Civil Service Act as the ''deputy head" of the department. Under section 31 of the Interpretation Act, he is the lawful deputy of the minister and can do any act or thing which the minister is empowered to do under any act or regulations.
With the reorganization of the defence staff, the problems of civil control will be very much simplified. The minister and the deputy minister and his staff will be dealing with one defence staff under a single commander. It will no longer be necessary to deal with three defence staffs, which has necessarily resulted in a good deal of the resources and energies of the civil staffs being applied to the problems of co-ordination. Civil control, as exercised by the civil staffs under the deputy minister either directly or through advice to the minister, cannot be exercised in a vacuum. It is essential that the matters over which the civil staff are to exercise control or provide advice do, in fact, come before them. With three organizations, each of which

has direct access to the minister, it is much more difficult to ensure that this does happen than it will be with a single defence staff. The changes proposed in the military organir zation in themselves will therefore facilitate the strengthening of civilian control.
In general the staff group under the deputy minister has a responsibility to the minister to see that the work of the department in all areas is carried out efficiently and economically. In other words it is their responsibility to see that the resources, manpower, materiel and money available for military purposes are used to the best advantage. To achieve this it is essential that there be a strong civil staff in the defence department outside the military chain of command for analysing and reviewing military requirements and the use of resources made available for defence. This requires a civil organization capable of reviewing and advising on defence estimates and programs.
Some changes will be made in the organization of civil staffs. As announced in the defence white paper, a program review system will be established which will provide for systematic review of all programs on a comprehensive basis covering a period of at least five years into the future. The object of this system will be to ensure that the programs being presented for the consideration of the minister, and subsequent changes to them, have been thoroughly analysed in terms of resources required to accomplish them, optional means of meeting the objectives, and the relationship to the total defence effort. This system is now in the process of being installed in the department but it will be perhaps a year before it is fully in operation. It will be necessary to some degree to reorganize civil staffs to handle adequately these new management arrangements.
In seeking to build a strong civil staff group to assist the minister in the control and management of the armed forces, I have clearly in mind the need at the same time for exercising care that the civil staffs do not assume functions which are necessary to the military staffs in order that they can efficiently control their military forces and carry out their military responsibilities. Both civil and military staffs have important roles to play and responsibilities to assume, and it is essential to efficient and effective operation that they work closely together and in harmony and understanding. I am glad to say that this is the case in the defence department today. I am certain that it will continue in the future and will, I expect, be enhanced as a result of the reorganization.

On the subject of civilian control I should mention the role of defence council. Defence council is chaired by myself or the associate minister. Its membership has included the deputy minister, the associate deputy minister, the chairman, chiefs of staff, the three chiefs of staff, and the chairman, defence research board. This council has been largely concerned with administrative policies in the department, and in the last several years has tended to meet infrequently and to exercise its influence in a limited area of defence activity.
As part of the reorganization it is our intention that defence council will become the departmental policy board at which all important policy matters relating to defence are considered, with a full interchange of views before decisions are taken. The exact membership of this council following reorganization has not yet been Anally determined, but it will include senior civil and military advisers to the minister. In order to permit it to do its work effectively the secretariat of the defence council will be provided by the deputy minister's staff. I am confident that this system will permit an effective exercise of civilian control and, equally important, civilian direction in the carrying out of defence policy as laid down by the government.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I really think it would be more appropriate to go into considerable detail once the bill has been referred to the committee, but the policy direction is that submissions and programs from the armed forces of Canada, after they have been analysed by civil staffs, will then be fully discussed by the senior military and civilian advisers to the minister in defence council before they are approved. This has not been done in recent months, certainly not during the last year, and I understand not in the years immediately preceding also.
Finally may I say, Mr. Speaker, that I think Canada has a unique opportunity, and consequently responsibility. The proposals put forward in the bill have been the subject of general discussions for many years and have been supported by many of the greatest military leaders of our generation. Their implementation would not be possible in some other countries at this time. In Canada, however, it is possible to proceed. We have often pioneered with new ideas in war and peace, and having proved their effectiveness
National Defence Act
set a pattern for future development. In the integration of our armed forces once again we are giving leadership in a very important area. As Canadians we have an inescapable responsibility to proceed with the plan and demonstrate its effectiveness.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say at the outset of my remarks that I find the minister has for once stuck pretty well to the rules of relevance, because he has limited his remarks precisely to the reorganization of the command structure of the forces. I think this was hardly in keeping with the spirit and the requirements of the house to discuss as a whole defence matters at this time. It is true that this could have been done on the resolution which the house approved a few moments ago, but I felt that the minister would have welcomed the opportunity to give us a general statement on defence rather than wait until his estimates appear, whenever that may be-some time in October or November, perhaps; we do not know.
I would also have appreciated an indication at this time of some of the observations he would have made regarding the interim report of the committee on defence. After all, the house has received no indication from the government as to its reaction to the white paper, other than in very general terms. The very general terms are, shall we say, the least courtesy which the minister could have offered. I may say that as a member of the defence committee I share his view about the report, that the work of the committee provided the members of this house with the opportunity to become much more familiar with defence matters and to approach the work of this committee in a real, nonpartisan manner and from a co-operative point of view.
If I may say so, as a member of the steering committee and as vice chairman of that committee I felt that we had developed a very flne spirit. My chagrin, however, has been that the government did not follow its good example of last year in setting up this committee as early in the session as possible. Seeing that the session commenced on February 18 I think it would have been quite conceivable to have set this committee up by March 15 and to have sent it along its way. I know that a goodly number of the members of the committee and also other members of this house wondered why this was not done. At least two months of valuable time has been lost. It may have been, of course, a question of timing, with the minister wanting to put forward his white paper first before

National Defence Act
the committee sat again; but I think a tactical error was made in this regard.
I agree with the minister's words that his white paper is but a charter or a guide, not a detailed and final blueprint. In commenting on the white paper today I am sure the house would not expect me to provide a counterblueprint. It is not of the type with which I seem to remember the minister in days past coming to the house, and which got a rather premature exposure much to his embarrassment. I am not going to go into that particular plan of 1959 or 1960, but from what I can recall certain things are now appearing which have some reference to that blueprint. So far as unification of the forces is concerned, at that time the proposal by the minister when he was in opposition was the appointment of a commander in chief.
In dealing with the matter of the appointment of a commander in chief I would refer the minister to the recommendations of the special committee of the house. The committee indicated that it wished to look into this matter further, and in this regard I think the minister might have been wiser if the committee had been permitted to sit earlier to look into this matter. I am most interested myself in this particular aspect. There are many people who have given this matter careful study whom I would have liked to have appear before the committee to give us the benefit of their years of study and their observations in this regard. In particular I might mention one man whom I have mentioned before, Mr. Richard S. Malone, who has written some very fine articles. I may not necessarily be in full agreement with him, but he has made a very careful study of the whole picture of the command structure of our armed forces.
I think it is here we have to start, and in my opinion it is unfortunate that there has come into the picture now the idea of the integration of the forces. We have started with unification of command, and the white paper speaks of this as the first step in integration. Here again I believe the minister has been premature, because the matter of integration of the forces is an entirely different thing from the unification of command. I would have been much more satisfied as to the wisdom of the government's decision if we had had the time and opportunity to look at the ramifications of integration in detail. There is a great deal more involved in integration of the forces than there is in the unification of command under one commander in chief.
I am wondering just where the minister has received his advice in this regard. True

enough his service chiefs will have assisted him, but I should like to know where he got his underlying motivation, inspiration and justification for integration of the forces; because it is quite clearly stated in the white paper that this is the aim. I would have liked to see a great deal more evidence on the pros and cons of integration. It is not sufficient for him to say "We think in our wisdom that we should integrate''. We want to know the reasons why there should be integration. We want to be able to discuss them.
True enough, an opportunity will come when the committee sits, because undoubtedly it will look into the white paper in great detail. But already the government is committed to this course of action, and surely we are not going to have the Minister of National Defence following the practice that has taken place in other sectors of the government in the last year of taking a major step forward and then having to back away from it. Surely we have a right to expect something else better than that.
The minister has taken a major step, but he has not disclosed to members of the house any really valid reasons. It is easy for him to say that it is in order to achieve efficiency and to streamline the operations, but that is not sufficient. We will have to have something much more than that. Again, I would have liked a little more detail as to the progress that has been made in this regard. The move was announced some time ago. Undoubtedly there has been a good deal of planning and there may have been some steps taken to this end. Can the minister give us a general timetable for the next few months as to how this will take place?
I have heard that the date of July 1, 1967 has been set as a sort of D-day for the completion of this program, or is it going to be U-day? Some people are saying that by this date everybody will be wearing a common uniform. We will leave that minor detail aside, but we would like to have more detail as to the programming in so far as unification is concerned.
The minister has indicated that he feels it will mean an over-all reduction of 10,000 service personnel. Will it also mean-I trust we can place this interpretation on his remarks-a reduction in the number of civilian personnel who are an integral part of national defence? We know there is and has been a very large civil staff, but if this move will merely mean that 10,000 people will put on their bowler hats in order to carry out the same jobs in mufti then there is little to be

gained by this transfer. It is true that the minister has indicated the move will mean a 20 per cent reduction in personnel on the administrative side at national defence headquarters, in certain of the supply units and so on, but this $100 million per annum reduction in what I would call the housekeeping or overhead costs will naturally have to be transferred for use in the purchase and maintenance of equipment.
The minister has not made a great discovery in this regard. I remember one of his predecessors, General Pearkes, expressing his concern at the time we were having special committees on defence expenditures. The service people who advised the former minister were quite correct. The actual forecasts and behaviour with respect to the proportion of defence expenditures have worked out as they forecast back in 1959 and 1960. There is nothing new there, and there has been no major discovery. The same problem is also present in the British, the Danish, the German and the French forces. Certainly this is always one problem. How much is it going to cost to house, pay, feed and generally cover the overhead of this outfit? I like to call these the general housekeeping expenses. Then we have to ascertain how much is left over to buy equipment.
There is a tendency for housekeeping to become more costly. I suppose it is like any domestic operation. As husbands we find that our domestic operations seem to cost more year by year, and there may be a tendency in this regard as well in national defence. The minister did mention certain things about retirement. I am going to leave this matter of unification with the criticisms I have made. I believe the plan has been disclosed prematurely without study by the committee on defence. I believe we could have had the advice of people outside of the minister's present advisers in this regard. I think we could have derived a good deal of benefit as a result of hearing all these views.
I fully agree with the fact that there should be unification. I understand that as a logical step. There is, however, one side of the matter that has left me somewhat puzzled; that, is the extent of the civilian control from the minister's own side of the department. Where is the independent yardstick to be applied by the Minister of National Defence? This has been a problem in the past, and unless I have misunderstood the minister's remarks I think this problem will exist in the future. It is true that there is to be the defence council. However, is it to be an independent body under the direct
National Defence Act
control of the minister which can apply that yardstick without having a responsibility for administration within the department? There is the minister, the associate minister and the deputy minister, but I am not too sure about the composition of the remainder of the defence council.
In order to really assess the situation I should like to see an organization that could give the minister independent advice. Witnesses before the defence committee indicated they thought that the commander in chief should be an adviser to the minister and not responsible for the administration of the armed services. It is true this does raise one question; how can you advise if you have not got responsibility? I will admit that this raises a problem, but where is the independent advice for the minister? After all the minister must then go to cabinet, and where is that independent advice for cabinet? This has always puzzled me; where is this independent advice? If anything is to be checked out, if anything is to be rejected or modified, is it done by intuition? Is it done for political considerations? Any time there has been a modification it has been given the mantle of a political modification, and I think that is wrong.
I know the minister is feeling his way in this regard. However, I suggest to him very strongly that there should be this independent, shall we say, control. The minister says it is part of the function of the civilian staff to provide some of the control, and the white paper mentions defence programming. To whom are these people responsible? Are they responsible directly to the minister without any intermediate responsibility through the deputy minister?
I am asking these questions because these are the things we should be asking in the defence committee before parliament is committed to this program. Unless the minister is able to give us these answers, I think he has taken a step without looking at a lot of these potential problems. Certainly they exist. These questions pop up in the minds of the members of the defence committee. I believe the minister had better be prepared to give us a full explanation as to how this is going to work; otherwise I believe all we will have had is a great shuffling, "plus ga change, plus c'est la meme chose".
I think the minister is aware of the problem I have put to him in this regard. How are you going to test the advice that is given to you? After all, the minister is not a professional military man. Usually the



National Defence Act
ministers are not. I think perhaps it is far better that he should not be; otherwise he is like the physician who is prescribing for himself, and that is not good at all. Let us find out how the minister is going to be be able to test and weigh the advice that he gets from within the service. I have discussed this with senior officers and they agree that there must be some form of examination, otherwise you may be so blinded by the justice of your own cause that you fail to see some of the difficulties. I hope that within this framework the minister is able to provide us with answers to these criticisms I have mentioned.
As a consequence of this reorganization the minister mentioned retirements. I suppose this is partly the answer the associate minister indicated would be given to the services today. What happens to those people who are being prematurely retired? They will be given a certain cash gratuity which is subject to tax. This is to compensate them in some way for the interruption of their military career and, presumably, the reduction in pension benefits they will enjoy under the pension act by reason of their shortened service. There seems to be one major restriction, that the cash benefit will not be paid to any service personnel who request premature retirement at this time.
I am wondering why that is so. I would have thought there were a number of senior officers and perhaps senior N.C.O.'s who may be two or three years away from normal retirement who could help the minister in his desire to reduce the forces by requesting that they go out now rather than wait out their time. After all, if they do so it must mean that they have an opportunity to resettle themselves in civilian life without too much dislocation.
I think in appropriate cases this should be permitted. After all, we have seen it in many another type of service in this country and other countries, in order to loosen out the top. I think the minister is faced with the problem of having a great number of senior officers, people of a certain age who have seen service in world war II. I believe there should be a loosening out in this, shall we say, rank structure. Why not give them the inducement to get out now if they have only a matter of a couple of years or three years to go to pension age, and let there be a waiver of the disabilities under service superannuation.
I now turn to other matters which the minister did not touch upon, but on which he has taken a lot of action since defence

was last considered in this house. The first is the militia, and I shall not go into that question in detail. Some of my colleagues will speak on it, but my particular interest concerns why the statement was made in respect to the reduction and reorganization of the militia when the defence committee had already set it aside as a special problem for examination. The committee's work in this regard would have assisted the minister.
The committee did plenty of work to assist the minister in what was probably the most urgent area, Europe. It was on that particular point that the committee concentrated its efforts, got the greatest amount of advice and offered the most numerous recommendations. I am glad to see the minister acceded in part to those recommendations, and I believe that strengthens my argument that it would have been better to withhold an announcement so far as the militia were concerned until the committee had dealt with that problem.
I can assure the minister there is a great deal of unrest in the ranks of the militia, unrest caused by uncertainty. If the minister wanted to carry out a reorganization of the militia, and I think one was due, it would have been preferable for him to set up the committee under Brigadier Suttie to examine the problem before making an announcement regarding what was to be done.
The minister made a grand announcement about the militia and the naval and air force reserves. Orders were issued that premises had to be vacated by certain dates, and no provision was made for the training of cadets. Because of that the orders were deferred, a review was made of the premises, and they are to be kept in operation until the end of June, when it is expected that we will get the report from the minister's committee or commission in regard to the militia. But why was there this sort of grandiloquent announcement and then withdrawals from it? The militia are most unhappy. This has left them up in the air.
What does the minister think about the survival operations training in the militia? Where does this fit in? The white paper has indicated that survival training and operations must be subject to the location of an anti-I.C.B.M. deployment, when and if that comes, and that no decision can be reached in the interim on survival operations. This is a rather unhappy state of affairs, and again it would have been far better to wait to see what the committee would bring forth, had it sat early enough this year to have gone into the question of the militia, survival training and survival operations.

I do not know how far the minister has gone in contacting the militia to get their reactions to this, but I can tell him that they are very unhappy. What about all our national survival and radiation control projects? Certain construction projects have gone forward and some have been interrupted. Officers have been posted as radiation control officers, but once they get that posting they have nothing to do. The whole thing is in a process of uncertainty. For the life of me I cannot understand why some of these decisions were announced in the manner they were and then the whole thing left hanging. Whether it was because of a certain desire to impress somebody that something was being done, I do not know. I do not even know that it has yet shown it is going to save money, because the cut-back of so many thousands in the militia is only a cut-back on paper, as the men are not there, and that means there is no saving of money. It is only when you cut back the effective strength that you are going to save money.
One of the things I hope the minister will be able to discuss with us was raised by the defence committee, with regard to the complexities introduced into his department by the existence of two ministers. I know this is a delicate matter and perhaps the minister does not want to step on the toes of the associate minister, but I ask is it absolutely necessary to have two ministers within the framework of the Department of National Defence? The administration of the department is great, but I would think it is still possible to organize that department on the basis of one minister and on one minister alone. I am not suggesting that the associate minister wishes to fire the Minister of National Defence or vice versa, but this is something fundamental, particularly when we are going to get a reorganization on a functional basis within the whole department.
Before terminating my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to join the minister in paying a tribute to the men and women in the armed services.
They have served well. A lot of them will no longer be needed. But I can assure this committee that many senior officers with whom I have discussed this question over the past year felt there was a need for change, a change in approach. Obviously there are likely to be serious dislocations, but I believe anyone who approached this question in a spirit of calmness and objectivity would realize that some changes were necessary in the Department of National Defence. Certainly changes were due with regard to
National Defence Act
some roles, and I will limit myself today to this particular point. I could cover a wide spectrum as far as Europe is concerned. I could deal with the militia in greater detail. I should certainly like to examine the role of our troops in Europe. But I will leave these matters to some of my colleagues who served on the defence committee and took part in the examination of those subjects.
I hope the minister in his closing statement will furnish us with much more information. I have tried to remain strictly relevant to the subject today although a wide open debate is permitted. It is for this reason that I am not touching on certain of the subjects I have mentioned. The contents of this bill are to be referred to the committee on defence, but here again there is a difficulty. The minister naturally wishes to go forward. He is asking us to go ahead right now. The committee on defence could say "We will leave this bill to the end." However, I do not think the minister would want that to happen. I would caution him, however, that I do not think the bill need come out of the committee very quickly. I say this because the measure has so many ramifications which will need to be examined. As long as the minister is reasonably patient with us, this examination can be carried out. As long as he does not want the bill back, say, in two weeks from now, the committee will be able to carry out its task.
I should like to know what deadline he has in mind as far as this proposal is concerned. I think we must be very careful about this, because the legislation now before us is the foundation of the whole structure and if we go wrong at this point we are likely to go wrong at many others. I for one would have preferred, at the present time, to have examined something else in the committee, but now the minister has forced our hands and I am a little unhappy about it.
There are others who wish to speak on this subject as well as on other aspects of defence. I had hoped the minister would give us a much fuller statement on defence matters generally than he did, because it is several months since he gave a report on these matters to the house and to the country.

speechtext:
We in
this party welcome the reappointment of the special committee on defence. The committee, as its own report shows, was well aware that it only scratched the surface in its investigation of the matters committed to it. In fact the report lists a whole series of subjects which in the opinion of the committee require further study.

National Defence Act
The very first recommendation of the committee was that it be reappointed early in the session. I must say I hope it was just an oversight or accident, rather than a reflection of the seriousness with which the government takes this committee, that in fact the committee is not being reconstituted until well into the month of May. I think members of the committee all feel that the committee could do a more useful job if it were sitting more or less continuously while parliament itself is in session.
In this party we shall support Bill C-90 on its second reading. In our view it provides a useful first step or piece of machinery looking to the integration of the armed forces; I think the hon. member for Edmonton West used some other expression, "concentration of command". Whatever it is, we think it is a useful first step. Indeed, in the light of the role which we see for our armed forces, a role I intend to discuss later, we believe that integration of staff, or integration of command, is not only advisable but absolutely essential. However, I should like to devote most of my remarks to expressing as clearly and vigorously as I can our disagreement-my disagreement-with the defence policy outlined in the government's white paper.
May I call it one o'clock? I am beginning a new subject.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I ceased speaking at one o'clock I had just explained that I intended to use the opportunity presented by this debate to say as clearly and vigorously as I could that we in this party disagree with a great deal of the defence policy outlined in the government's white paper. When the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made his famous speech in Scarborough in January, 1963, he said that his party felt bound to honour the commitments made by the previous government to acquire tactical nuclear warheads for our army brigade in Europe and for the strike reconnaissance squadrons stationed in Europe, as well as for the Voodoos and Bomarc missiles attached to NORAD. At the same time, however, he promised a thorough examination

of the whole basis of Canadian defence policy. I would like to quote his words on that occasion. This is the Scarborough speech of January 12, 1963, in which he said:
The government should re-examine at once the whole basis of Canadian defence policy. In particular it should discuss with the United States and with NATO a role for Canada in continental and collective defence which would be more realistic and effective for Canada than the present one.
This examination would be concerned, among other things, with the necessity of building up NATO's conventional forces and the part Canada could play in this.
A little later he said:
In the full re-examination of defence policy, and in which all parties could participate through a defence committee of the House of Commons, a Liberal government would be guided by the following considerations:
I will not read all the considerations, but one of them was this:
Our financial resources are limited. Therefore we should be careful to see that our defence dollars are spent sensibly and economically, avoiding commitments which require expensive equipment that is, or soon will be obsolete; and activities that are, or soon will be, meaningless.
Later, if I am not mistaken, I heard the Prime Minister say in this house that the tactical nuclear commitment that he said had been made by the previous government was, in his opinion, a mistake. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) himself when in opposition wrote an article which was published on January 25, 1963 in which he explained the defence policy of the Liberal government. This article was in a paper called The Varsity Weekend Review, and in it, as one might expect, the minister supported the stand taken by the Prime Minister at Scarborough. He added these words, however:
One of the questions which bothers many sincere people is this: Will not the fulfilment of our commitments now make it impossible for us to pursue anything but a nuclear role in the future? The answer in my opinion is a resounding no.
In the future we will be able to adopt the policy which we think is most in keeping with our national objectives. Once the policy has been agreed on, however, we will be expected to fulfil it without equivocation.
Then he said:
The other question people are asking is why we bother to fulfil our commitments when we intend to negotiate new ones in due course.
He goes on to explain that:
Only in this way can we earn again the right to speak forcefully in the alliance. Second, renegotiation implies consent of our allies, and when agreement has been reached the implementation of a new policy cannot be achieved at once-it is physically impossible. It will require, at best, several months for a new government to adopt a sound, long range policy and present it to our allies for

concurrence. It will take several years to Implement the new agreed policy within the limitations of orderliness and a reasonable level of defence expenditures. In other words, by the time a new policy could be implemented in full our present commitments would be honoured in full, and the equipment we now have would have served its useful life.
Consistently with those two pronouncements by the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence, we in the defence committee, the members of the house, and indeed the Canadian public have heard from time to time about this proposed re-examination of Canada's defence role. We were led to expect that out of the white paper would emerge, I think it was called a bold, new policy for Canada that would set a new course for Canada's defence posture for a decade. It is our view, Mr. Speaker, that the mountains have laboured and produced a mouse. The white paper contains some sensible and useful observations and a few good suggestions as to the machinery, but when it comes to the re-examination of Canada's role, the white paper evades the issue. It calls for nothing more than a continuance of policies based on a strategy which in our opinion is obsolete, provocative and dangerous.
The white paper has had a very good press. I suspect the reason for this is that many of our editorial writers and commentators seem to know little and care less about the problem of defence. I do not expect to gain any particular popularity in those circles by saying this, but the facts speak for themselves. The general public has been led to believe that the integration of the services which is proposed by the white paper and which is partially implemented, or perhaps a better word would be foreshadowed, by the bill before the house will result in substantial reductions of the defence budget. Indeed, in my own home town we saw screaming headlines in the newspapers the day the white paper was announced declaring a $100 million cut in defence expenses. In all fairness the white paper does not pretend to say any such thing. Page 19 is very much more modest. It says this:
Thus, integration will result in a substantial reduction of manpower strength in headquarters, training and related establishments, along with other operating and maintenance costs. The total savings to be effected as a result of such reductions will make available funds for capital equipment purchases, and eventually make possible more equitable distribution of the defence dollar between equipment and housekeeping costs. Sufficient savings should accrue from unification to permit a goal of 25 per cent of the budget to be devoted to capital equipment being realized in the years ahead.
National Defence Act
The goal is, therefore, that 25 per cent of the expenditures should be devoted to capital equipment. But the special committee on defence-and I assume the information they had was accurate-makes this statement in paragraph 39 of its report:
Evidence presented to the committee shows that approximately 77 per cent of Canada's total defence budget, 1963-1964, is allocated to the payment of salaries and to expenditures concerning maintenance and operations, while only 23 per cent of the budget is for new equipment.
I do not know whether the phrase "new equipment" as used there is the same matter which is referred to as "capital equipment" in the white paper, but if it is you will notice, Mr. Speaker, that the aim of the white paper is to achieve a shift from 23 per cent to 25 per cent. While that is a laudable, worth-while objective, the size of the change is not very remarkable.
A close examination of the white paper indicates that if-and I emphasize the word if-its recommendations are carried out it will involve a substantial addition to present defence expenditures. The white paper proposes a series of what it calls major expenditures and these are new expenditures to be made largely in the next few years. Page 24 of the white paper says:
On the basis of this assessment, major expenditures in the next few years will be designed to:
(a)	re-equip the army as a mobile force;
(b)	provide an adequate air and sea lift for its immediate deployment in an emergency:
(c)	acquire tactical aircraft;
(d)	maintain a relatively constant improvement of maritime anti-submarine capability.
Those are praiseworthy objectives and I am not opposing them in any way, but I do say that if we continue our former commitments and then add these new expenditures which are proposed in the white paper we shall be adding to the burden of taxation of the Canadian people in regard to defence rather than reducing it. And this will be at a time when the responsible leaders of most of the other major countries of the world are in fact reducing their expenditure on defence.
I know the minister confined himself to the bill, but he did not touch on what is the major problem facing Canada in the matter of defence, and that is that we are in my view faced with a choice of roles in the field of defence. I think it is the tragedy of the white paper, and the weakness of the policy of this government, that no choice is made between the options but that the government seeks to do both things at the same time. One option, as I see it, is to go on doing just what we have done before, that is

National Defence Act
a process of escalation which will then end in the suicide of a mutual strategic nuclear holocaust.
Another thing that has changed the views of those concerned with strategy is recognition of the fact that the myth of a vast Soviet superiority in conventional forces was just that, a myth. Mr. McNamara made that abundantly clear in his speech in November to which I have already made reference.
I suggest that our strike reconnaissance force is particularly dangerous because it is vulnerable. The incentive in a moment of rising tension for one side or the other to strike first is so great, they cannot wait to be sure whether or not war is coming. There is an ambiguous act that may mean war, and the advantage of destroying the other person on the ground before they have destroyed you is so great that the situation may well get out of control and an unintended nuclear holocaust would follow. Indeed, in my opinion that is the main danger of war at the present time. There is very little danger of anybody being so crazy as to attempt the suicidal course of a planned nuclear attack on Europe or North America. This is highly improbable unless we assume a degree of insanity that does not exist. What is less improbable is that, with this confrontation of massive power set up in Europe some incident will arise and tension will grow and the temptation to release a striking force first will be so powerful that the thing will not end until there is the destruction of our civilization.
We were told in Europe-when I say "we", I mean the defence committee-by the wisest observers, that the strike reconnaissance role should not be carried out by aircraft based on the ground because they are too vulnerable. It should be carried out by Polaris submarines which can afford to wait. There is no incentive to use them immediately for the purpose of averting a threat by striking first. If only submarines were used in this particular instance one could afford to wait to make sure the threat is unambiguous, and war is real. Even the ability to wait a few hours could make the difference between destruction of the world and non-destruction. Why do I say this? I say this because even a few hours many enable political wisdom and common sense to intervene and the disaster of all-out war would be prevented.
What does the white paper say about this strike reconnaissance role? It says nothing but that we should carry out what we have been doing. What does it say about our contribution to the front line? It says we should maintain our present role in Europe, but it
tMr. Brewin.]
points out no military reason for doing so at all. It alleges political necessity for doing so. It is suggested that if we pull out of the front line and cease carrying on this particular role, somehow or other we will undermine the whole idea of NATO and the morale of the European countries.
I want to make it very clear I am not advocating the total withdrawal of our forces from Europe. As I have said already, our intervention forces such as I have recommended, could play in my view a much more useful military role than the role we are playing at the present time. I agree it would be a mistake to do anything that might imply disunity or weakness in the western alliance. However, I suggest it would be a sign of good sense as well as strength if Canada and her NATO allies were to move towards easing the political tensions in Europe by ceasing to rely upon tactical nuclear weapons as an immediate response to any threat in Europe. I am not suggesting they should be thrown into the sea. I am suggesting they be withdrawn well behind the line, where they would not be used early in any conflict which arises. Canada's contribution to European defence is probably one two hundredth of the whole. I suggest it is a little ridiculous to suggest that, because we move out of a role that I suggest is dangerous and no longer necessary, somehow or other that would undermine the defence of Europe. After all, Europe is not what it was when we first sent our troops to NATO. Europe has grown stronger and grown more prosperous. She is perfectly well able to look after her own commitments although, as I say, the contribution of an intervention force to deal with problems which, according to the information we received were at the top end of the spectrum, the things most likely to happen, such as probes in Norway, in Denmark, in Turkey or Thrace-
