speechtext:
You have proposed in your white paper two brigades and you propose to equip them more effectively to play this intervention role. I think that is a good idea,

and I have said so. However, I do not believe you can do that and carry on this other role which at one time the minister himself thought should be re-examined, and of which I believe he was just as sceptical not very long ago as I am myself.
I must say that the white paper reminds me of the old case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, the person with the split personality. I do not know whether the minister claims authorship for the entire white paper, but I read somewhere in a newspaper that he was the main author. Certainly, he accepts responsibility. I find interspersed between sensible and perceptive observations, some good suggestions with weak and evasive conclusions. There is, however, one good thing about the white paper, and that is it makes a virtue out of flexibility. I hope the policy is sufficiently flexible to enable the government to move quickly towards the adoption of the sort of defence policy that we in this party recommend. We recommend a policy and role which is realistic and distinctively Canadian, a policy which we think is commensurate with our means and our aptitudes, a policy which is needed in the world, indeed in the alliance. We believe that this policy would be consistent with an international policy based upon the strengthening of the United Nations and its peace forces, a policy based upon the urgent need for making progress in disarmament, particularly in the difficult but dangerous confrontation in central Europe.
Lastly, we believe that this is a contribution that Canada is particularly fitted to make because it cannot be made in the same way by the major powers or the former colonial powers. We think that we can make it and we should concentrate on making a contribution to these peace keeping forces through strengthening the United Nations and eventually building in that way a world order. The government has moved in that direction and I commend them for it, but they have not had the courage to break off from the old things they were doing before. I venture to suggest that if you try to do both of these things together, you will find yourselves on the horns of a dilemma and one or the other will have to go. I am afraid that as long as you stick to these old commitments and do not boldly say they are obsolete or outdated, and we have to get out of them, then I do not think you are likely to make a really effective contribution to the peace keeping forces about which the Prime Minister himself has spoken so eloquently in his speeches and about which he has written in Maclean's.
National Defence Act
I think that this white paper is a disappointment in that it promises us a bold new policy, but it advances haltingly and inadequately towards that policy. It fails to grasp the facts that it should have grasped. I hope the flexibility it promises means that the government is still open to give real reconsideration to the role that Canada should play in defence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We
welcome this opportunity today to participate in the debate on this very important subject of national defence. It does not seem as though these opportunities present themselves too often. We do hope that in the course of this particular debate we shall be able to discuss a great many related subjects and we will not be confined to the particular measure that is actually before the house. My understanding is that a fairly wide range is permitted in this debate at the moment and I shall proceed, therefore, on that basis.
Many references have been made and are being made today to the apparent relaxation in international tension. We certainly hope that there is some basis for these particular statements. On the other hand, in view of all the considerations we dare not be lulled into any feeling of false security, so I believe the maintenance of a relatively small but efficient defence force is essential at the present time to remind any potential aggressor that we will not tolerate any violation of our national borders nor any infringement of our sovereignty. In addition to that responsibility of defending our own borders, we have the broader participation in the North American defence operations, and the still wider responsibility of making our contribution to the defence of the free world.
As has been pointed out, during the course of the last session the special committee on defence was established. I believe that generally people look upon the establishment of that committee as a very worth-while project. Many people who have given some attention to the matter would agree very satisfactory work was done by that committee during its sittings last year.
Just prior to Christmas the committee tabled a report, which had been prepared somewhat in haste and without having the time to complete a thorough study of all the relevant problems. Nevertheless, that report does make some definite recommendations. I do not want to take up the time of the house today by reading the list of the various items to which the committee felt attention must be given.

National Defence Act
It is rather extensive, and there was no desire on the part of the committee to intimate in any sense that it had completed its assignment.
The general feeling among committee members was really that we had just commenced our studies, and the iterim report that was submitted contained just a few of the recommendations that were more or less obvious ones. With regard to a great many other important matters, the committee felt a lot of them were of such magnitude that it was not in a position to make any definite recommendations with regard to them. Therefore it submitted a list of these other matters which it decided should be considered when the committee was reconstituted.
As I say, the committee made certain specific recommendations, but having listened to the minister's statement today I wonder if he thinks they were very important. In fact the general attitude of the minister has been rather discouraging, so far as the work of the committee is concerned. He has given us his blessing. He has stated that every cooperation would be given the committee, but yet in a great many instances we have found that he has proceeded to forge ahead in certain fields that the committee felt should be thoroughly studied before any action was taken in them.
In other cases the minister has indicated somewhat of an impatience with the work of the committee, and that he had to move ahead himself because, in the final analysis, it is his responsibility to make important decisions. For that reason I wonder whether the minister places any great reliance upon the recommendations of the committee, or whether he has any practical appreciation of the work that the committee has been endeavouring to do.
The main item which is before us today is Bill C-90, which has to do with the unification of command. In paragraph 27 of its report the committee made mention of this particular matter as follows:
In order to follow up the second chapter, further time is required to study the following matters:
(a)	Integration and co-ordination of the armed services.
(b)	Role of the militia and other reserves.
(c)	Compulsory military service.
(d)	Manpower management.
(e)	Service colleges.
(f)	Civil defence.
This shows the committee felt sufficient study had not been given to this particular matter of unification and integration, and it suggested that when the committee was reconstituted it would be able to give its time and attention to a more thorough study and

analysis of this particular problem. But now we find the minister moving forward, introducing the amendment having to do with this matter, thus showing neglect and a repudiation of the position of the committee relative to such a study.
The minister made a statement and referred to the necessity for a long range, coordinated defence policy. He stated that the moves that were anticipated through the introduction of this amendment were just part of this long range, co-ordinated defence policy. We certainly hope the time has arrived when we will have a co-ordinated, long range defence policy, because so far as the people of Canada are concerned they have been very dissatisfied. They have wondered just what the policy was, just what direction we were heading in, and what it was all about, because there did not seem to be any clear enunciation of defence policy in a manner that would enable them to understand what the minister and his department were trying to do in this particular matter.
Reference was made this morning to savings, and I would like to find a more adequate word because it was pointed out that this was more in the nature of a transfer of certain funds from one part of the budget to another. It was pointed out by one of the previous speakers that the percentage of the defence budget for overhead expenses was so far above the amount of money allowed for the procurement of new equipment that it was very badly out of balance. Reference was made to the matter of a 25 per cent, 75 per cent, and so on ratio. I can understand why the minister wants to make some correction in this particular matter, because it was pointed out by a number of the witnesses who appeared before the committee that there was a serious imbalance in this matter, and that more of the defence dollar should be spent on the procurement of new equipment with a consequent lowering of the percentage allowed for overhead and maintenance.
The minister also made reference to the provision for those who would be retiring prematurely because of the reorganization of the defence department. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) raised the question as to why there should be some discrimination regarding those who may want to retire and who express the desire to retire prematurely. If we are going to dispense with the services of a certain number of personnel then I do not know why people who may wish to retire prematurely should be penalized. It could be done on a voluntary

basis and then the balance of the forced retirements would make up the total figure envisaged. I do not think people should be penalized and deprived of this consideration just because they would prefer to retire earlier.
This whole matter will have some effect upon the employment situation, upon the ability of individuals to secure gainful employment. Every precaution should be taken and every consideration given to see to it that those who are going to be displaced in this particular manner will not suffer unduly because of the change of policy. I wish to say right now that I agree with the proposal which is before us. I think it has been under study for a considerable length of time. I believe there are many aspects of it which should be analysed before we move forward with the whole program, but I believe it is a move in the right direction. Further, after discussing this matter with a great many people across this country, in the services and outside them, I have come to the conclusion that there is general support for a move of this kind intended to make the operation of our defence establishment more efficient.
Without question a radical change in defence thinking and planning is taking place. This has been made imperative as a result of the changes which have been taking place in weaponry and political alliances. Therefore, it is necessary that there should be a degree of flexibility, as far as defence planning is concerned, so as to keep in step with these various changes. Speaking personally, I think we should commend the minister for the initiative he has shown in taking hold of a difficult situation. In spite of the fact that his actions might not have been acceptable in some circles, he had the courage and the initiative to go ahead and propose changes which I believe have been due for a long time.
As we consider the problem of defence generally, as far as Canada is concerned, I think we find ourselves in a special position, or a difficult position, because Canada with a huge land mass and a relatively small population must find it hard to meet every situation which could possibly arise relative to her defence. I do not think it is easy to plan in these circumstances. I do not think it is easy to envisage the situations which may arise in the future and exactly how we ought to prepare to meet them. For this reason, as I say, I believe a certain degree of flexibility is necessary, and the fact that
National Defence Act
the minister has indicated his agreement with this view is to be commended.
I shall not attempt to elaborate this afternoon the policy which we in this group have advanced from time to time, except to say that it seems as though the ideas we have suggested and which we have in mind are gradually being recognized and that at least some of the proposals we put forward are being adopted. I do not say we can take any credit for that, but at least we had the vision to put forward some of these ideas which are now being taken up and implemented. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) who spoke before me, said the government was taking a halting step in this direction. Well, I believe halting steps are better than no steps at all. The direction in which we are moving at this time and the proposals which are being made indicate that the government is moving on a course which is, I believe, acceptable to a great many people across the nation.
I should like to read a brief paragraph from a statement made by our leader, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) stating defence policy. He said Canada's objectives should be the creation of a strong, modern, completely mobile and efficient force. I think that sums it up succinctly. We still believe this should be our objective. Canadian forces must be adequate to maintain surveillance of our skies and coasts and also to meet any emergency which may arise. However, we have a wider responsibility. I believe it is essential that we should continue to co-operate with the United States in measures for the defence of the North American continent. This was pointed out, I believe, in the committee's report. On page 758, the recommendation is that Canada remain a member of NORAD since the defence of North America is a joint responsibility. I believe this is essential because, as I have indicated, Canada, with its vast land area and small population cannot hope to meet the challenge which would be imposed by any massive aggression. We must, therefore, depend to a large extent on our neighbours and, in turn, we must be willing to make our contribution to the extent that it is possible in the defence of North America.
Moving further afield, there is a necessity for continued co-operation with our NATO allies in the field of collective defence. This subject would possibly lead us into a discussion of nuclear arms and nuclear commitments. I do not intend to go deeply into that now, because the views of our group have already been set forth in this respect.

National Defence Act
Here again, if we interpret correctly the tenor of the evidence given by witnesses before the defence committee and, somehow, project the nature of the move being made on the part of the government, it would appear we are leaving the nuclear field, now, in favour of a more conventional type of operation. We think this is to be commended. Indeed, we have advocated it through the past years.
The United Nations remains, of course, the universal organization to which is committed the maintenance of peace. In this connection we have supported and continue to support the contributions which Canada is making because these, after all, are part of national defence. In contributing in any way to the maintenance of peace in the world, no matter where the peace may be threatened, we are contributing to our own national defence. The world today is getting smaller. We can no longer think of it as segments separated by so many miles or days. The world is shrinking and becoming exceedingly small. Therefore we believe that in continuing our support of the United Nations and its peace keeping operations we are making a contribution to the defence of our own nation as well as to the peace of the world.
I just wanted to make these few remarks about the bill which is before us and about the whole subject of national defence. Others of our group will be speaking on this subject. We do think it is necessary to maintain, as I have said, a strong, well equipped, modern mobile force because we believe that in this way we can best defend this nation and make our contribution to the defence of the North American continent as well.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in respect to Bill No. C-90 with which we are dealing, we understand from the different expressions we have heard and from looking over the bill that it is concerned with an integration of the armed forces and concentration of command. These expressions apply very well to the subject we are discussing, but the bill itself is mainly concerned with the concentration of command. We also have the information given us by the minister in the white paper on defence, which I imagine is a summary of his ideas on the establishment of a military program, and so forth. Coupled with that we have another summary of the white paper. This makes three summaries. I will probably try to summarize them, so on the whole these summaries may be very lengthy. I
[Mr. Patterson.)
shall try to give a summary of the summary of the summary in order to arrive at what should be done in this matter of defence. If the minister will refer to Hansard he will see that on Friday, December 9, 1963 I spoke on this matter to a certain extent, and I do not intend to repeat what I said on that occasion. However, I will reiterate a few of the points I raised at that time, especially concerning the integration of the armed forces.
Before dealing with that matter I would like to say to the minister that in my opinion this bill should be a little more extensive.
I know it is a starting point, but the starting point is not quite correct, as I understand the position, because today we are talking about the naming of the chief of the main headquarters and, if my information is correct, he has been named already and is leaving tomorrow with the delegation for Colorado Springs. I will let the minister answer that one and say whether I am correct. Also, I gather that the headquarters will still be in Colorado Springs. I have always understood Colorado Springs to be in the United States and I do not imagine its location will be changed in any way after we have named the chief of the main headquarters. I have a suspicion that not only the minister controls that office, but also some of our good and willing neighbours sometimes give us a helping hand, which I would say is not always to our own benefit. If we are to have a command which is completely Canadian, I do not see why we have to establish it in the United States. This is one point about which the minister should be concerned and should endeavour to bring this command back to Canada. We and the United States have to work together as an international power. That is okay; but working together means we must also be able to make some of our own decisions.
We have been discussing the integration of our forces, and quite a few question marks pop up as we consider this problem. In fact, some objections were made in this regard last summer when we were on a NATO tour of different military bases in Europe. These objections were raised by some of the high ranking officers and were on this basis. When we spoke with somebody in the navy, he had his views on it. Then we went over and saw somebody in the army. He had his views on it, and his views were different. Then we went and saw somebody in the air force, and he had different views on it. We found that these views are not always the same. The navy would be willing to be integrated completely

so long as they were allowed to keep their traditions and customs. This also applies to the army and the air force. This is one thing the minister has not discussed in the white paper. Perhaps he has an idea of what he is going to do in regard to the necessary coordination. In fact, Mr. Speaker, on page 19 of the white paper on defence we find the following passage:
Two objections are given as reasons why integration should not be undertaken. First, that morale or "esprit de corps" is weakened, and second, that competition is diminished. Neither of these objections will stand against careful scrutiny.
The last one, namely that competition is diminished, can probably be overcome because I do not see how two Canadian armed forces such as the army and the navy can be competitive when they are trying to defend their own skins. There might be some people like that, because there is always pride in one's force, but I think this could be overcome. With regard to esprit de corps-and this is the most important of the two considerations- I think we can imagine the esprit de corps of the Canadian army as a whole, but there are different points which are going to be very ticklish to deal with. Whether you integrate or not, you will still have an air force, a navy and an army, and the guy who is undergoing army training is not riding on the boats or ships. The man in the navy is going to be boasting about the ships, and the man in the army is going to say how good it feels to be on solid ground. I think these are two different fields of activity which could be commanded by one general headquarters, but the soldiers or the bottom men will still have their own feelings and in my opinion will always keep them. This was one of the main objections raised by the military people themselves. They were wondering whether they were going to be given the same uniform. This is one thing the minister has not mentioned, although I may not have correctly understood what he said. You cannot have complete unity if you start producing a distinguishing effect with the uniform. Is the navy, the army, or the air force going to have a distinctive uniform, or will they all have the same uniform? Also, you have the civilian men in the army. They also have rank and qualifications. How are they going to be considered in this whole set-up? The minister has probably considered this matter, but this is one fact that we bring to his attention.
The minister this morning spoke mainly about saving $100 million. It is always good to save money, but if we are going to save money, or amend or change something, we must do it for the benefit and good of all.
National Defence Act
I agree with the minister about concentrating the integration of the armed forces under one command, but the way to go about it is what I would like to know about in more detail.
There is another thing upon which I commend the minister. In fact, I spoke about it on December 9. This is a subject dealt with by the hon. member who preceded me, and this was in the Social Credit platform. I refer to making the armed forces very effective, very mobile and versatile for our own uses. It is useless to consider joining the nuclear arms race that exists across the world. First of all, we cannot afford it, and second, by the time we have a nuclear war engine ready for operational use the thing will be obsolete and somebody else will have produced something new. It is no good our trying to keep up in such an arms race because we will always be three or four years behind the rest. So in regard to nuclear warfare we are about as useless as can be on a competitive basis.
I am glad the minister has understood this and is turning his attention toward another way of protecting the Canadian nation and also fulfilling our commitments throughout the world. We can do this by having very effective conventional weapons and also by training people to use them most effectively, not only in wartime but also in peacetime. This is also the goal of the armed forces. Quite a time elapsed between the two world wars, and the armed forces have been maintained since at great expense, just in case there was war. Some people say, if we want peace prepare for war. I think Caesar said that, but I still do not believe in that principle. I think if you want peace you also have to prepare for peace, and in peacetime the army has a role to play just as much as in wartime. It can be used in peacetime as a deterrent force. In wartime it is used as a defensive force as well as offensive; but it is mostly used defensively to protect this nation.
But in peacetime when we are not defending ourselves what are we doing with our armed forces? What are its members doing besides keeping their boots and buttons shined? We can give them something to do to build the country economically speaking instead of their being just an expense. We can use the army as an internal force to help the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. We can use it in time of fire or floods. It is already used to a certain extent in this way but we can use it even more. These forces should

National Defence Act
be trained to be ready for action at any time of emergency, either in Canada or wherever help is required. It was ready when Cyprus needed it, as I could have told this house before.
In fact I spoke about that on December 9. I spoke about Turkey, having just returned from a tour of that country. Turkey is one country in the world which has one of the longest histories of warfare, dating back thousands of years. If Turkey had spent just 10 per cent of what it has spent on warfare and devoted it to other matters it would be one of the most beautiful countries to visit, as well as one of the most prosperous. But at the moment the economy of Turkey is very weak, a fact which the Turks express openly. Greece is not so much stronger, and they have the same sentiment towards war. When these two countries do not have a common enemy they fight between themselves. I do not know whether they are just trying to keep in practice, but soldiers should not be used only for fighting. We can also use them for something else, and the minister should tell us something more of his plans in this regard. Has he any definite ideas about using these armed forces later on, not only as a means of defence but also to help the country either in production, in protection, or in any way the minister wishes to consider?
I was talking a moment ago about trying to save a few dollars and perhaps I can assist the minister on this. I want to mention a matter which concerns Uplands airport and it relates to a practice which is common to a large extent right across the country in different fields, wherever government administration is concerned. At Uplands airport there is someone controlling the purchasing of transistors for transistor radios. Uplands airport purchase these transistors in lot purchases, although I do not know how. I also do not know why they need to use two men in a three ton truck to collect a transistor from a certain store in Ottawa. That is one matter the government should look into, because if it is done here it is probably done somewhere else as well. I do not know who authorizes these purchases, or who authorized two men and a three ton truck to go to a store and get a radio transistor.
There are also at Uplands electronic tubes which are used in television sets. I do not know how many televisions there are at Uplands airport, but practically anyone on the base can just about go into the storehouse and get a radio or television tube without saying where it is for use or for what instrument. A lot of these technicians come into [Mr. Langlois.l
town and do repair work as a sideline, and I would be interested to know where they get their television tubes. I would like the minister to check into this. I am not trying to state facts; I am just raising question marks. In fact, the minister has given us a lot of question marks so I am giving him a few back.
There is another matter which I should like to relate in French so that I do not get mixed up with technical terms. If the minister would listen and answer when he speaks I should be very much obliged.

Could the minister check up on this: Apparently, there is some buying of electric and electronic wire from an American firm to repair electrical and electronic equipment in Canadian planes. It would seem that the company purchased the wire after it had been discarded by the U.S. air force.

If we are going to turn around and "buy American" this is beginning to be expensive. Therefore I should like the minister to check on that matter too.
These are all details which I am relating to the $100 million savings the minister was building up to. It is right to save, but we have to save all round. I should like the minister to check into these matters and to see whether there is any leak, because if he can prevent some sort of scandal it would be a lot cheaper to remedy the matter immediately.
The minister says the armed forces in Canada are to be transformed. We have to have concentration of command and integration of forces. But we also have to consider the preparation of our armed forces at the level of the militia cadets. I do not know how the minister is going to establish these cadet bases, but he might also take them into his consideration.
Militia courses are being given in my region, for example. The cadets are to be transported some 70 miles in the morning and some 70 miles back again at night, a round trip of approximately 140 miles. They will be trained during the day and brought back at night in this course which commences in June. According to the local authorities, with many more than 20 cadets it would be much cheaper if the training were done right on the spot, with the instructors there.
I do not know what risk the government will have to assume under the present plan or how much it would cost the government if: one of these cadets was injured in a car

accident. Has that point been considered? I know that some of the parents have complained about the plan. They would rather have the training done at Thetford Mines than for these cadets to be transported 140 miles every day.
I imagine the minister will solve these small problems when he gets around to them, but this one problem in my region may very well pop up somewhere else throughout the country. If we want to interest our young men in becoming cadets, let us not start out by discouraging them the first time they undertake military training.
I should like to refer to page 20 of the white paper, where reference is made to a recommendation of the royal commission on government organization in these words:
The government accepts and will implement the recommendation of the commission "that the deputy minister be given greater responsibility for keeping under review the organization and administrative methods of the Canadian defence establishment, and assisting the minister in the discharge of his responsibility for the control and management of the armed forces."
I should like to discuss this matter briefly. This is one thing that is not in the bill. If there are going to be changes in the functions or powers of the deputy minister we should like to know exactly where we stand. We have in Canada a nation that is looking foward to a peacetime defence organization that will also provide adequate protection and efficiency in wartime. But I know one thing is true. The Canadian people will support the government in its work in this regard as long as it does not interfere with the economy too greatly by being too expensive for the country. If that should happen you can be sure that the government will not have the support of the Canadian people.
I think that is one reason why the Canadian people were so much against nuclear weapons. We could not afford them and they knew it. But we can afford to pay and will pay for a very efficient, versatile, mobile armed force, whether or not it is integrated under one command. It is the minister's problem to see that the forces co-operate and work together for the protection and maintenance of peace in this country.
