speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is inescapable that a deplorably small percentage of our military defence budget is being used for the procurement of new equipment. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) mentioned that he thought the figure was in the neighbour-20220- I96i
National Defence Act
hood of 23 per cent and therefore increasing it to 25 per cent was not very much. I suggest to him that the figure of 23 per cent includes the construction of new buildings and does not apply only to new equipment.
What has happened in the past ten years is that, from a high in 1954 of 42.9 per cent of our defence budget devoted to the purchase of new equipment, we have this year come to the point where only 13.3 per cent is being devoted to the procurement of new equipment. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, if this trend continues for another couple of years we will have well paid, well dressed and well fed forces but with the poorest equipment in the world. For this reason I am sure we all agree that this imbalance has to be corrected.
Another thing I like very much in the white paper on defence is the emphasis on mobile forces. I do not think this is shown any better than in Cyprus. Within a very short time from the time parliament gave its approval for Canadian troops to be sent to Cyprus they were landing on that island. But the reason that our troops were able to get to Cyprus so quickly is that Cyprus has an airport with hardened concrete runways that can take the Yukon transport planes that we have in Canada. The Yukon aircraft requires long hardened runways and fortunately Cyprus has them. Therefore I am very happy to see that, while we have acquired some already, the white paper calls for the acquisition of more C-130E Hercules aircraft.
The reason I am so happy is that this aircraft, with its different aerodynamic characteristics, can take off and land on relatively short and unimproved air strips. We have mobile forces that we can use to fulfil our NATO commitments and to assist the United Nations in dealing with brush fire wars, but I am afraid it will happen quite often that we will be wanting to send them to places that do not have excellent airports like Cyprus. There will be other places in the world to which we will want to send our forces for use by the United Nations in putting down brush fire wars, places that will not have airports of this type. Therefore I believe it is a very sound step to procure the Hercules C-130E short take-off and landing aircraft.
There has been some talk about not preparing for war and that this does not help to keep the peace. In that regard I should like to read a few words from the conclusion of the white paper. It states as follows:
Force alone, as all history shows, is not able to establish an enduring and creative peace. Nevertheless, and regrettably, it is essential to maintain force on our side as a deterrent against attack from

National Defence Act
potential foes who are themselves heavily armed; as a means of removing the greatest temptation to an aggressor, the assurance of easy victory.
The maintenance of adequate force for the above purpose gives us the time in which men of wisdom, persistence and good will can work together to build a world where peace will be secured by stronger means than force. If we fail to take advantage of the opportunity that time gives us, then peace, and with it civilization, may be lost. If we spare no effort in seeking for peaceful solutions to the problems that divide and embitter men, then true peace may be established and all mankind gain the victory.
I feel that all members of the house agree with the work done by the defence committee last year and with its establishment this year. I say; Let us have second reading of the bill as soon as we can, send it to the committee and let the committee continue the work it did last year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to say I am disappointed in the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) because of the way in which he introduced the debate today. This is what comes of attempting to make an arrangement to forgo the debate on the setting up of the defence committee in exchange for a general debate on the bill introduced by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer). We expected him to make a complete statement with regard to the defence situation in this country. Having made that arrangement, the Minister of National Defence simply talked on the narrow issue of the bill itself. I think he has performed a disservice to parliament and to the country in this regard.
We have not had a full debate on the problems of defence for five months. This is one of the most important areas of consideration, and a full statement should have been made by the minister today. This is the thing for which we were waiting, and this is what we did not get. It was on that basis we agreed to forgo the debate on the setting up of the committee. We could have had two debates and stretched them out for several days. However, we did not want to do that. We want to get on with the business of the country. However, before passing the bill or setting up the committee, we wanted to have a full disclosure of what has been going on in the field of national defence. The minister had his opportunity and did not take it. Once again he has failed to perform his duty, as I see it, because a heavy responsibility rests on the Minister of National Defence and on the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) of this country.

I noticed that the minister told us the Prime Minister was in accord with his proposals in the white paper and in this bill. We were so encouraged to hear that the Prime Minister approved of what the Minister of National Defence was doing. What if he had disapproved? The Prime Minister does not approve of things that are being done by some of the other cabinet ministers, but we are now informed he approves of what the Minister of National Defence is doing. Obviously, he is the white haired boy of the cabinet. Then, the minister did as he did in December, he praised his associate minister. The associate minister will get up and praise the Minister of National Defence. This is what was done last December. They pat each other on the back and say, "My, how hard my colleague is working." They are the gold dust twins working together, struggling with these great problems. They are burning the midnight oil and producing a white paper.
What else have they produced in the course of the year that they have been in office? This is what we wanted to know today. We asked questions all last session with regard to national defence, but we could not get very satisfactory answers. One year has elapsed. What about the Prime Minister's promise that after closing the nuclear gap, to use his words, he would then negotiate Canada out of the nuclear field? What has happened to that in the course of a year? We have been very patient. We have been waiting for this diplomatic action. What has happened? The Minister of National Defence failed to tell us. Is this another broken promise by a promising Prime Minister? I wish the Prime Minister were here to give us an answer to this question. Why does he make these promises to the Canadian people and then fail to fulfil them? This is a question that is being asked right across this country. Promise after promise, tailored to suit an election campaign, has been made and then there has been the failure to fulfil these promises. What did the Prime Minister mean when he said he was going to undertake immediately to negotiate Canada out of the nuclear arms area? Obviously, he meant nothing.
Why does the Minister of National Defence not tell us something about the Bomarc, how much they are costing and things of that nature?
If we believed for one moment that the Bomarc provided any real protection with or without nuclear warheads we would concur in their use, but we do not believe so-

In our minds it is not a question of using a missile with an atomic warhead such as the Bomarc. It is our conclusion after serious consideration that in the time period in which these missiles will be in operation they will provide no effective defence whatsoever and might just as well not be there. If anyone else thinks differently let him support the policy and let him pay the piper. We do not believe so.
These were the words used by the Minister of National Defence speaking in the House of Commons in August of 1960 when he was a member of the opposition. What has been done with the Bomarcs since he has undertaken responsibility for them? He had no use for them then; he was not going to pay the piper. Who is paying the piper now? Who is in control? He said:
We particularly do not believe so when the atomic warheads would be under the control of the United States government.
Are they under the control of the United States government now? We have not heard one word from the minister with regard to the Bomarcs for which he had no use, according to words attributed to him on page 7572 of Hansard for August 4, 1960.
What about the Voodoos? Would he tell us the number of squadrons he has, and are they armed with nuclear missiles? Where are they stationed? What protection are we getting from the Voodoos in Canada? We have not heard one word from the Minister of National Defence. What about the Star-fighters?
It is true that we do have two air bases in Germany and presumably F-104's could operate from them. In the day of missiles, however, it would seem sheer folly to station eight squadrons of atomic equipped planes on two bases where they are vulnerable to sneak attack. We urge and demand that the government communicate to the house exactly what plans it has for the effective use of these machines.
These are the words used by the Minister of National Defence on August 4, 1960, when he was a member of the opposition, and they appear at page 7565 of Hansard. We have not had one word from the minister with regard to Starfighters. In December I asked him questions about the Bomarc, Voodoos and Starfighters. I said, let us know if any one of these Starfighters in Europe is equipped to fight. I got an answer on the order paper here not so long ago to the effect that they were not equipped. This air division in Europe could not fire a shot, so far as we know today or tomorrow if called upon to do so.
Now, I said the Minister of National Defence has heavy responsibilities and so has the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister has to take responsibility for the defence of
National Defence Act
this country and, through his cabinet, he is responsible to the house and to the people. What is the state of readiness of our forces? One year has gone by since the election campaign at which time the present Prime Minister was saying we did not have any Starfighters in Europe equipped. He said there was a whole air division flying around in Europe not equipped to fight. There was not an air division then; there were only 18 planes. Of course, they were not equipped and we acknowledged that. A year has gone by, and is that air division fully equipped now?
What about the bases for the nuclear weapons for these F-104's? How many of them are there on ready alert, ready to take off at a moment's notice? How many are still stationed in France on bases where nuclear weapons, apparently, cannot be used? What teeth have the air force, except those in the police dogs that are guarding the missile dumps that have not yet been constructed. Is that all our air division in Europe is doing? Just a few years ago it was the elite air force in NATO, but the present Minister of National Defence wiped out the Sabre jets which were fully equipped to fight and were ready for action, at any time over a period of ten years. What is the air division in Europe doing now? Why did the minister not tell us this afternoon? Surely this is important. What purpose is served by having armed forces unless they are ready for instant action? That is the type of Minister of National Defence we are saddled with.
I hope the minister will give a reply to that in due course, or that the associate minister will do so when he gets up to compliment the minister and after he has finished patting him on the back.
With regard to the defence committee, everything I said about it in June last when we were setting it up has turned out to be true. I said I feared that matters of policy would be decided by the government without reference to the committee on defence. That happened. I said that I feared the committee on defence would be discussing various matters, hoping to evolve some advice for the government, and the rug would be pulled out from under it when it was involved in those discussions.
I can give two examples. The frigate program was cancelled by the government after the defence committee had been struggling with the problem for several days, getting evidence, examining figures and talking to the admirals, but all the time the Minister of National Defence and the associate minister

National Defence Act
had their hands on the rug. Suddenly they gave it a yank and that work done by the defence committee was just useless. The frigate program had been cancelled, but there was not one word to the committee while this was going on.
Subsequently the minister decided that there would be a serious curtailment of the militia forces of this country and, without referring this subject to the committee on defence, he appointed a committee, gave it instructions to bring in a report, and removed this from the subjects for discussion by the defence committee. What purpose can be served by a committee when it is treated that way?
During the course of one of our discussions here I asked the minister if he wanted advice on policy matters from the committee, and he said no. That was a very interesting day in committee when he said he did not want advice on policy. We were just to inform ourselves so that we would be able to participate in discussions on defence matters on the high level of the minister and the associate minister. Like groundlings, we were to emerge from the pit and get up on the stage if we had the information.
Now we are again setting up the defence committee. Is the minister going to refer problems to us? Will he let us discuss the question of the militia before the decision is made, or will he pull the rug out from under us while we are discussing that problem? Is there any use in our discussing it? If he has got all the answers and the decisions, what is the defence committee to do? That is the difficulty that we face. In my opinion the future of the defence committee is problematical and I wonder whether it really can be effective under those circumstances.
If I heard him right, the minister said that the bill presently before the house, if second reading is approved by the house, will go for consideration to the committee on defence. In other words, he is determining the subject matter that will be placed before that committee, because obviously a bill of this nature would have to be looked at and discussed soon. We would not want to delay it indefinitely.
I was interested in the reports we received month after month about the study the minister was undertaking, and the production of the white paper. We had more advance information with regard to that white paper than we had with regard to the production of the motion picture "Cleopatra." Week after week we were told, "A white paper is coming out; all your problems will be solved."

Then there were leaks of information as to what was to be contained in the white paper. Then there were inevitable delays because the minister was still studying the subject. It took him a whole year, or certainly ten months, to produce the white paper. Then it came out with a great glare of publicity. The highlights were presented for people to look at. It was described as a ten year plan, the "first such long term defence plan." The late Hon. Brooke Claxton, if he were now living, would not agree with that because he had long range defence plans, and so had his successors in office.
Then we had a list of the highlights in the white paper, as though there were something absolutely new and different in it. Some of the commentators indicated to the public that now at last Canada has an understanding of the goals of her defence policy. I know, Mr. Speaker, you know this, but strangely there are others who might not, namely that there have been other white papers. This will come as a surprise to a great number of people, but we have had white papers in existence, to my knowledge, from 1954-55 up to 1961, and there were some before that.
I have read all of these white papers and in many respects they are superior to the one for which we had to wait almost one year. In 1954-55 the Hon. Brooke Claxton published a white paper setting out Canada's defence objectives. He said:
The objectives of our defence policy remain the same as heretofore:
(i)	The immediate defence of Canada and North America from direct attack;
(ii)	implementation of any undertakings made by Canada under the charter of the United Nations, or under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or other agreement for collective security;
(iii)	the organization to build up strength in a total war.
Defence policy was known to the minister of national defence, to parliament and to Canada as far back as 1954-55. A white paper was prepared each year after that, but I pick out the one prepared in 1959 by Hon. G. R. Pearkes, Y.C., on the subject matter of defence policy. Fancy, talking about defence policy as far back as 1959. One would imagine that it was only in 1963-64, under this minister, that the subject of defence policy has been studied, perceived and disclosed, but back in 1959 we read this in parliament:
Canadian defence policy derives directly from our foreign policy-
You will find a sentence like that in the present white paper.
-and is designed to ensure national security and the preservation of world peace. These objectives

are reached through collective arrangements within NATO and the United Nations.
Then, skipping a few sentences, I read this in paragraph 2:
In order to meet the objectives of the alliance and in support of the United Nations, it is the defence policy of Canada to provide forces for:
-The defence against an attack on the North American continent:
-The collective defence and deterrent forces of NATO in Europe and the North Atlantic:
-The United Nations to assist that organization in attaining its peaceful aims.
Well, there we are. Defence policy has been spoken about in this house and written about in numerous white papers. It has been expressed and re-expressed. And now, in March, 1964, we have a white paper on defence which is supposed to be the final word-the new look. This is a discovery which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) has made-a discovery of defence policy. He suggests to us in a foreword:
The objectives of Canadian defence policy, which cannot be dissociated from foreign policy-
These words are familiar in the light of what I have been reading.
-are to preserve the peace by supporting collective defence measures to deter military aggression: to support Canadian foreign policy including that arising out of our participation in international organizations, and to provide for the protection and surveillance of our territory, our air space and our coastal waters.
Then, on page 6, these objectives are listed again under letters (a), (b), (c) and (d). Here they are:
(a)	Collective measures for maintenance of peace and security as embodied in the charter of the United Nations, including the search for balanced and controlled disarmament;
(b)	Collective defence as embodied in the North Atlantic treaty;
(c)	Partnership with the United States in the defence of North America;
(d)	National measures to discharge responsibility for the security and protection of Canada.
I would be interested if someone would disclose what is new in this white paper. It is rather a good literary document. I think it was drawn up by officials in the Department of External Affairs or in the historical section of the Department of National Defence. Now and again, the minister has got in a word of his own; he has a few words which I recognize here and there. It is a carefully drawn document. There is an introduction and the objectives are stated. Then there is a historical summary of our policy since 1945, followed by considerations affecting our future and a section on the organization of the defence forces. Then the minister looks ahead for ten years to the
National Defence Act
shape of Canadian forces between 1964 and 1974, and follows up with a section dealing with defence research and industry. Finally, just in case people might be too critical, he provides an escape hatch through which one could drive 12 Centurion tanks line abreast, because by means of this escape hatch he could get out of anything he had said in the pages earlier.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is that the part attributed to the minister?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes. These are the exact words, I think. I recognize the minister's style in the conclusion, assisted by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin).
Well, that is the white paper. I suggest it is a most incomplete document. I was tremendously disappointed in it. In a white paper, in addition to a literary exercise setting out objectives and things of that nature, we require-and all previous ministers recognized this requirement-tables and charts showing the size of the forces, the expenditure of money over the years, how the defence dollar has been distributed, and so on, so that all who are interested may be able to form a picture of what has been going on. There is nothing of that kind in the present white paper on defence. It is simply a literary exercise. It contains only one thing that is new, and I intend to deal with that in a few moments. Why were we not favoured with summaries of expenditure and charts to show where the money has gone? This has been mentioned before but it does not hurt to mention it again- in 1954-55, 21.3 per cent of the defence dollar was spent on military personnel and 42.3 per cent on procurement and equipment. By the time we had reached 1959-60, military personnel costs had risen to 33.1 per cent and money spent on the procurement of equipment had gone down to 21.3 per cent. You cannot have it both ways. You cannot increase the personnel in the armed forces and raise their pay and allowances, as we did when we were in office, without effecting savings somewhere along the line, unless the entire amount available for defence is increased.
Why did the minister not put things like that in the white paper? Why did he not give us, as was done in 1961 in a booklet published under the name of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness), a summary of expenditures for the past ten or 15 years, so that we could make comparisons? This would have been very helpful.

National Defence Act
In 1952-53 total expenditure on national defence amounted to $1,882 millions in round figures. In subsequent years it was $1,805 millions, $1,665 millions, $1,750 millions, $1,759 millions and then $1,686 millions. The minister talked about a saving. He says he has effected a saving. I would point out that we effected a saving of almost $262 million in defence expenditures as shown by the record for the year 1958-59 when defence expenditures totalled $1,424 million. This is not the first time there has been a substantial saving in defence expenditures. The figures carry on. Expenditure in 1959-60 amounted to $1,514 million. For the next five years I have no figures for final expenditures, but I have estimates. These are the estimated expenditures for the following five years: 1960-61, $1,520 millions; 1961-62, $1,614 millions; 1962-63, $1,590 millions; 1963-64, $1,634 millions. The minister is now proposing for 1964-65 an expenditure of $1,525 millions.
These figures give the house a proper basis for comparison. Now a serious decision has to be made with regard to the amount of money to be devoted to Canadian defence, and parliament has to look at this question very closely. Are we to set a figure of $1,500 millions and stay there? If we do, what are the choices. One course which might be followed is to reduce the percentage of the defence dollar spent on personnel. The other is to reduce the amount spent on the procurement of equipment, operations and so on. This is the problem which is facing the minister. He talks about financial savings. He told us-and I objected to his use of the word "savings" in that connection-that he had brought about a saving of $100 million in the estimates as is shown by the figure I have just read. But what the hon. gentleman is really doing is transferring a saving realized by reducing the cost of military personnel, headquarters establishments and so on, to the purchase of equipment. To say otherwise is to mislead the public. I noted, by quickly going through the estimates that out of the $100 million he mentioned the hon. gentleman has made a saving of $80 million on equipment, the very item we were going to spend more money on because, he said, we were falling behind. In other words he has cut out the purchase of equipment by the navy, army and air force to the tune of $80 million. Then, in order to get that back for the purchase of equipment he has to cut down on personnel.
That is about what he is doing. He is chopping down personnel in order to find money to spend on equipment, because he has

reduced the over-all budget by approximately $100 million. Well, he has to maintain the efficiency of the armed forces while doing that. No one will object to the saving of money through the reduction of unnecessary overheads. I suggest, though, that more information will have to be given to us as to how this is to be done. The minister has talked loosely about the integration of our forces; articles have been written about it, but nobody completely understands what is in the mind of the minister with regard to that and he did not explain it this afternoon. What does he mean by "integration" of our forces? He should have given us a discourse on this. It is not clearly set out in the white paper. How far is this integration to go? It is a desirable objective. It was started by General Pearkes in 1959. He started on this program of integration by reducing the staffs in the medical, chaplain and recruiting services. That is where the start was made, and we have to carry on from that point. How far is integration to go?
The minister is starting with the report of the Glassco commission which recommended a change in the chiefs of staff committee. He mentions this in the white paper; but the white paper failed to quote all that the Glassco commission said with regard to that proposed change. Let me read from page 73 of the Glassco commission report:
In relation to the key function of the chiefs of staff committee of advising the minister and the government on military aspects of defence policy, the C.C.O.S. has no formal pre-eminence and there may be merit in making this function the collective responsibility of the committee.
I draw attention to this sentence:
Excessive concentration of the advisory task in the hands of one man has obvious dangers.
The Glassco commission did not elaborate on that sentence. The minister does not mention it in his white paper and made no comment on it today. I think parliament has to look very, very closely at that to see whether or not it is advisable. I do not think there will be opposition to integration, but it is the question of how it is to be done. That is the function of this house, to examine the method by which that integration is to be accomplished and how far it will go. If it means placing too much control in the hands of one man, which the Glassco commission has already warned is dangerous, then we must watch exactly what we are doing with the bill which is before us.
I would refer the minister to some comments on the government white paper by Brigadier Malone. This article was published

in the Winnipeg Free Press. I seldom have occasion to quote the Winnipeg Free Press and they seldom have occasion to mention me, but I am not unfriendly to Brigadier Malone in his capacity as a former military officer, and I know he had practical experience in warfare, has made a great study of the theory of warfare and was very much interested in the militia. Brigadier Malone has drawn attention to the fact that there may be a serious danger in the command structure as envisaged by the proposal of the minister. I have not time to read the various things he has put in front of us in articles in the Winnipeg Free Press, but I draw attention to his suggestion that a study should be made of the findings of the royal commission on defence under Lord Esher in England in 1904. I have made that study. He says that the proposal now put before parliament by the minister is reverting to a system which was found to be unacceptable by Great Britain in 1904. They had had plenty of experience and found that it did not work. Instead of that, they set up a defence council, different from the one the minister mentioned this afternoon, and in this connection Brigadier Malone says:
What Is required today is a defence council at the top policy-making and administrative level of which the chief operational officer of all three services is but one of the members.
He is not the supreme commander-inchief; he is just one member of that council. Then he says:
The other members (of equal authority) should not be divided according to separate service but as to the other main functions or divisions of defence. The council should include, as well as the senior operational officer-
That is the supreme commander:
-the senior officer responsible for all supply, transport, accommodation and equipment, etc. (for all three services), the senior administrative officer responsible for such services as recruiting discipline, legal, welfare and so on. These officers should speak with equal authority to the operational chief of the three services and they should take their orders not from a supreme commander-in-chief but from the defence council itself.
There is not time for me to extend these remarks with respect to this particular feature of it, but I do suggest that before we launch too far into this sea that the minister is sailing we should observe the experience of the past and the marked reefs. The army organization in England in the 19th century, in the Crimean war and the Boer war, foundered on the mistake of having a supreme commander-in-chief, as Brigadier Malone points out, and they corrected that mistake by setting up an army council-the same
National Defence Act
applied with regard to the navy, and so on- in which the supreme commander-in-chief was only on an equal footing with other people who had the administrative services under their wing, and there was the proper civilian control, which was not available in the days when the supreme commander-in-chief looked after everything.
So I sound this cautionary note at this time for a consideration of the matters drawn to our attention by Brigadier Malone, for a study of the Lord Esher report, for a study of the system operated at the present time in the United Kingdom, so that we do not, in the haste for reform, make what might become a very serious mistake.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the bill now before us.
First, I wish to refer to the re-setting up of the special defence committee. I think we are unanimous, in this house, in supporting that measure and in saying that this committee has already played a useful role and is called upon to play an even more useful one this year and in future. I should like to point out that the members of the committee constitute together a most valuable storehouse of technical military knowledge. Therefore, it would be in the interest and to the advantage of the house to use the special knowledge acquired last year by the hon. members who took part in the work of the committee. We should, as much as possible, keep the same members.
I believe that is the policy followed with respect to defence committees in most countries of the alliance that we visited last year as members of the committee. I am thinking in particular of the French committee on defence which is composed of members of the national assembly and which has been under the chairmanship of representative Moinet for many years. In view of the continuity of its membership, the committee has been most helpful to the French government in the establishment of a military policy.
Consequently, I take this opportunity to impress upon hon. members the advisability of reconvening the committee on the same basis as much as possible.
I should now like to deal with remarks made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) when he introduced his resolution. He referred in particular to the savings which would result from the new plan to integrate the armed forces. I do not intend to dwell on the subject, since my colleagues,

National Dejence Act
the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre in particular, dealt with it and pointed out that in spite of the reference to savings made by the minister, no savings will be effected actually, because the government has no intention whatsoever to reduce the appropriations for military purposes any more than it has already done. No attempt should be made to delude the public with a plan designed to look as a means to effect savings in that field, when no savings are actually being considered.
Mr. Speaker, the minister spoke of the immense advantages that would result from integration; for instance, it would reduce the number of people or channels of information reporting to him, which would give him a better interpretation and a better co-ordination of military information-that may be true-and would give him a better opportunity to set up on a functional basis the Canadian armed forces.
But why did the minister, when he spoke about integration-of course he is well known for his modesty-speak of it as if he had discovered something extraordinary, a new planet for instance? If you analyse his speech thoroughly, you might be led to believe that before him no one in Canada or in any other country had thought about the need to integrate the military forces.
Mr. Speaker, it is well known that this project has been under consideration for many years by military authorities, by the former minister of national defence, and that everybody agrees today, because of modern military technology, that integration is necessary.
Integration is the first essential step toward the streamlining of our armed forces. How could it be otherwise when today the role of the various services being integrated, has become undistinguishable.
This is the age of space ships. Because of this, we can no longer separate the army, navy and air force and assign each service a special and air-tight role.
Therefore, what the minister suggests is only the first unavoidable step in that direction. What he puts forward is not a fait accompli and there again I do not understand the minister who, in a very pleasant tone of voice and without passion, reveals to the house things he would like us to believe are extraordinary but which are the most normal in the world. That outline he gives us remains more than just an outline. Even if the integration of the armed forces should become a reality, what the minister is suggesting 
at this time is not the massive integration of our military forces but just integration at the top, replacing three chiefs of staff by a single one. That is far from the complete integration of the armed forces which would be desirable.
Moreover, the minister shows us integration as being desirable from an administrative point of view and also for purposes of economy. It might very well be, but if integration has become necessary it is certainly not because, from the administrative point of view it might be more flexible, or because it would be cheaper from the economic and financial point of view; but it should be at least for the purpose of making Canada's military role more efficient and more flexible to apply.
The minister also referred to the necessity of maintaining civilian control over the military forces. Who, in this house or outside, questions that necessity? But the minister has a special art for presenting his ideas and projects as if they were the result of the fullest deliberation and that his projects become absolutely necessary due to exceptional circumstances which he does not fully reveal to us.
Really, listening to him this morning, I thought for a moment that we were on the point of witnessing in this country a coup d'etat plotted by a military junta. This comes from the way the minister outlined quite normal things, in order, I believe, to set off the splendid role he laid out for himself.
Mr. Speaker, we are of course in favour of a control of military forces. I do not think there is any reason to believe that the minister will lose this control. If there is such a danger, I think it would be his duty to resign and surrender his functions to another who would apply this control; otherwise, we would be like those republics where democracy is but window dressing.
This is not the situation in Canada, except that I was somewhat upset, Mr. Speaker, by this week's developments. I am thinking especially of the melodramatics of which Kingston was the scene when the royal commission of inquiry on bilingualism and bi-culturalism met in that city.
The situation was judged so unusual-and I insist on that word-that the commanding officer of the area felt it necessary to issue special orders to forbid members of the Canadian armed forces in the district to attend the sittings of the commission or, at least, to participate in the discussions.
My colleague from Royal (Mr. Fairweather) looked up the military regulations in that

respect and he found no substantiation for those orders. The Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin), who is paying close attention to me, changed the regulation by saying that such questions were controversial and that the military personnel should in no way be involved in controversial discussions.
Mr. Speaker, surely the fact of being a soldier in peace time Canada, does not mean that you have to abstain from publicly discussing topical matters of general interest which, if they are subject to controversy, certainly do not jeopardize the security of Canada or other military objectives.
I am not at all satisfied, Mr. Speaker, with the muzzling of our Canadian military forces on this occasion. In fact, I am very dissatisfied with it and, when reading the minister's explanations, people might think themselves right in the middle of a who dunit starring Maigret. Anyway, that was the impression I had, and which seems tome normal under the circumstances.
Therefore, I understand the better, or rather still less, the motives of that military commander, when I think of some briefs submitted at that commission sitting, for instance, the brief of Dr. Arsene Lauziere, professor of French literature at the Kingston military college, on which the Minister of National Defence and the Associate Minister of National Defence did not make the slightest comment.
I believe that, because of the seriousness of the charges made by a person in authority, the Associate Minister of National Defence, who is more particularly in charge of personnel, might have given some explanation to the house. Some very serious charges have been made. It has been said that in the army, the current language, in which everything was done, was English; that promotions were slow and difficult for a French-speaking officer, and finally, that, if you wanted advancement in the army, you had to learn and speak English. Moreover, though the French language was allowed for communication in the Royal 22nd, even that regiment had to use English when communicating with other units.
Mr. Speaker, there must be a very good reason for this state of affairs, but the house is entitled to an explanation, especially now that tremendous efforts are being made to convince French Canadians that they constitute an integral part of this nation and that they are on an equal footing under the confederation pact.
National Defence Act
I think that, in this matter, the minister can, if he wishes, and not only if he wishes, but it is his duty to do so, take very useful action. I do not think that what was reported by the professor is false, because I, myself was a member of the national defence committee and I was in a position to know that in Europe, particularly at the Canadian brigade base in Germany, children of French Canadian servicemen were receiving their education exclusively in English. No effort was being made either to follow the curriculum adopted by the province of Quebec, because the course given was different, or to have French classes for children of French Canadian servicemen.
Now, I am saying this with great objectivity, for I think that such a situation is abnormal. I merely mention it in the hope that the minister will very shortly take necessary steps to correct this anomaly.
Mr. Speaker, this brings me back to the national defence policy of Canada. While we are considering this defence bill, we are entitled to ask what is the general defence policy of Canada and what is the trend of that policy in regard to objectives set in the field of Canadian foreign policy?
Those well-known objectives aim at maintaining the sovereignty of Canadian territory and curbing communist expansion, as far as we can and finally, at maintaining order among nations.
Those are broad objectives, and to attain them, Canada participates in some essential alliances, the principle of which must never be questioned-and today more than ever before-of joint defence for western nations. That is why we are and will remain within the Atlantic alliance, as well as the North American alliance. We are also a member of the United Nations, and for those purposes, we contribute to the maximum of our means; this has to be in order to promote disarmament and raise the standard of living throughout the country, notwithstanding our foreign aid program.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock? [Text]

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Order. It being five o'clock the house will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely, public bills.

Broadcasting Act BROADCASTING ACT

the second reading of Bill No. C-25, to amend the Broadcasting Act (political programs).
He said: The purpose of this bill is twofold. First, it reduces to two days the restriction now governing political broadcasts prior to a federal election. As every member in the house knows, at the present time political broadcasts may not be made on election day nor on the two days preceding election day, that is from Friday midnight until the night of the election. This regulation, of course, governs broadcasting, but the newspapers may carry political advertising even on election day.
This amendment I propose will give the broadcasting media, that is radio and television, a more equitable arrangement as compared with the newspapers, but it still does not equalize them. The present Broadcasting Act says that no licensee shall broadcast a program, advertisement or announcement of a partisan political character on any day that an election is held for the election of a member of the House of Commons, the legislature of a province or a council or municipal corporation or on the two days immediately preceding any such day. As I have said, this refers to a federal election, a provincial election or even a municipal election.
I know many hon. members have had the experience of having broadcasts from parliament hill cancelled because there was an election in some other area. I know that during the last election in Newfoundland I had a broadcast cancelled which I did not really believe was of a political nature.
The second purpose of the bill is to ensure that the prohibition mentioned above would only apply to a broadcasting station within the broadcasting or receiving range of the electoral district involved. This provision would not apply, therefore, to federal elections because all of Canada would be involved. However, it could apply to by-elections, provincial elections or municipal elections. This sounds a little complicated, Mr. Speaker, but it can be done since I am told that each broadcasting station has a licensed pattern or range.
Apropos of what I have just said, I should like to quote from Hansard for August 26, 1958, where the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), at that time
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Batten).]
the minister responsible for the C.B.C., was discussing Bill No. C-55 regarding the establishment of a board of broadcast governors. I should like to quote from pages 4115 and 4116:
I do not know how many hon. members know this, hut under C.B.C. regulations as they apply today if there happens to be a town council by-election in Wolfville or Port Albemi, then the C.B.C. is not supposed to broadcast political programs for three days prior to that by-election although there may be a provincial general election in Ontario. That is the existing regulation which has application to federal, provincial or municipal elections. The thing is just silly.
A little farther down on the same page, I find this:
After a great deal of discussion we felt it might be allowed to stand this way; the elections committee of the House of Commons would be set up in the relatively near future and that would be a much better forum in which to discuss this question and arrive at some solution with respect to political broadcasts and so on, rather than attempting to deal with it by way of amendments or by a board outside the control of parliament.
Speaking in the same debate later, as recorded on page 4129, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings said:
It was the understanding when we inserted it here rather reluctantly that this was not the place to include it but as this certainly was not the time to engage, as I said before, in a prolonged political discussion about advertising and programs it was put here, shall we say, as a temporary resting place until the elections committee could meet.
This referral mentioned by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings at that time has never taken place. I went through the reports on privileges and elections and ascertained that in 1959, a year later, this topic was mentioned by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). However, the committee never proceeded with it. In 1960 the committee did discuss a 48-hour prohibition on political broadcasting. After a great deal of discussion they felt they should leave the regulation as it was. After reading the evidence and trying to deduce the reasoning of the committee at that time I found they felt television had a greater impact on the general public than newspapers and therefore it was reasonable to leave the newspapers with the advertising advantage over radio and television. During the meetings in 1960, the committee discussed amendments to the act concerning political broadcasts from outside of Canada, that is broadcasts originating across the border. At this time amendments were proposed, which were accepted later and became part of the Canada Elections Act.
The committee on privileges and elections met in 1962 and 1963, but this topic was not

discussed. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the consideration of this matter by the committee which was promised in 1958 has never been undertaken, for one reason or another. I am introducing this bill at this time in order to bring to the attention of the house the fact that this matter should be considered and I hope that members of the house will refer it to the committee on privileges and elections, as should have happened in 1958.

I shall not detain the house very long, Mr. Speaker, but there are a few comments I should like to make on this bill. I should first like to deal with the clause concerning dramatization. In my opinion this has been a sore spot so far as a number of people in Canada are concerned. I feel that dramatization, especially those in which the candidate takes part in the discourse, are a means of getting a point across. It seems to me this is merely a matter of education so far as the individual who is viewing the program is concerned. After all, this is the point of a political broadcast. Surely, the cost of a broadcast on television is high enough, so that the best use of that time should be made in order to get a point across to the viewer.
I should like to refer now to the free time for political broadcasts. I believe the voter is entitled to hear from each party on an equal basis in order that he can ascertain for which party he should vote. I am very strongly opposed to the situation where, because of the number of members in the House of Commons or the number of people who voted in the last election, one party gets the lion's share of the free time provided on television. I am strongly opposed to the situation where a party, because of its numbers in the House of Commons or because of the number of people who voted for it in the previous election, gets the lion's share of the time given by the taxpayers themselves to view the various parties' positions and the things they have to present to the public. To my mind that is absolutely the reverse of what it ought to be.
We should look at this whole matter from the point of view of the viewer, and the ability of that individual to get a much clearer picture in his mind as to where he should put his "x" when the vote is being taken.
I would like to refer just briefly to broadcasts outside Canada. We may say that we can regulate this from Canada, but I say that any person who wants to get somebody else in the United States to give a very
Broadcasting Act
strong viewpoint, over a United States station, in connection with a Canadian election can probably do more to emphasize a position than if the people of Canada themselves could go across the line and put on a program. The reason I say this is because it would be an isolated incident that would stand out from the rest of the broadcasts at which the viewer would be looking.
We have to be big enough and bold enough so that we can stand in the face of all competition, and put our wares before the Canadian public as much as we can so that they may be able to decide for themselves what they are going to do when election day rolls around. In closing I wish to say I would very much like to see the subject matter of this bill referred to the privileges and elections committee where it could be gone into very thoroughly and perhaps, out of that, could come some badly needed corrections.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to indicate briefly the support I have for the bill which has been introduced by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley). The remarks just made by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe), which of course deal with a section of the act that it is not proposed to amend by this bill, serve to emphasize the desirability of having the general subject matter of the bill sent for review and study before a committee, where the views advanced by the mover of the bill and the hon. member for Cariboo could be gone into.
I am not quite sure how the name of Port Alberni happened to come into this discussion. I was not in the house when the minister made the statement which was quoted by the hon. member for Halton, but I mention it merely to emphasize the fact that this is a subject which, at various times and under various circumstances, has come up for discussion in Port Alberni in connection with elections to the various levels of government.
While the basic idea of having some restraint or limitation on partisan broadcasting in the period immediately preceding an election is a good one, it is ridiculous that the act is so worded that it prohibits broadcasts, where there is overlapping, for elections to the various levels of government. It is ridiculous that a report from parliament hill may have to be cancelled because of a purely local election in that region of the country represented by the hon. member who contributes to the report. I am sure most hon. members who have participated in these broadcast reports have had that experience.
The hon. member is to be complimented on presenting this bill. I certainly hope the

Broadcasting Act
subject matter will receive early consideration in the appropriate committee of the house, so that out of that will come a recommendation that the anomalies which exist with respect to broadcasting in other jurisdictions will be removed from the act.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support the bill of the member for Halton (Mr. Harley) now submitted to the house, because it points out an absurd situation which can result from the application of section 17 of the Broadcasting Act in its present form. In fact, it is entirely illogical to note that a candidate in a federal election or even an elected member called to express the point of view of his party on radio or T.V. may be prevented from doing so, because a simple municipal election is going on elsewhere in another part of the country, sometimes quite far away.
Therefore, I congratulate the member for Halton for having set forth the principle of the bill under consideration.
I also believe that he is entirely justified in submitting this bill to the committee on privileges and elections, because I feel it is not only section 17, but the whole Broadcasting Act that should be completely reviewed.
Mr. Speaker, it is not simply a matter, as proposed in this bill, of reducing the period of time to three days, when no program of a political character could be broadcast prior to a federal election. There is more to it, and that is why I suggest that the whole Broadcasting Act should be reviewed.
A rather difficult problem arises at election time. It happens that all radio and television networks are congested with political and partisan speeches, and this becomes boring for the listener or the viewer. This is likely to cause serious prejudice to politics itself and to depreciate, in the eyes of the people, the idea of greatness and nobility of political competition that every responsible citizen should have.
Therefore, the principle now before the house enables us to consider other amendments, like the one I just talked about, to the effect that the board of broadcast governors could exercise the rights it holds under section 1 of the said act which authorizes the board of broadcast governors to exercise a more effective control on political programs during election campaigns in order not to supersaturate televiewers who cannot but listen to often boring political speeches broadcast on radio and television. In my opinion, there is a problem there that should be considered.
[Mr. Bamett.l
Mr. Speaker, another problem comes up, particularly in the province of Quebec and in Quebec city.
Through CFCF-TV station in Quebec, political programs of a separatist nature are broadcast every week by one Leo Tremblay, a true paranoiac who constantly attacks confederation and federal institutions. There is also the leader of the RIN that my hon. friends opposite have the opportunity like me to hear and who preaches secession from confederation.
I am in favour of the absolute respect of democratic procedures, in favour of the fullest freedom of speech, but I have the right to denounce an obvious violation of section 10 of the Broadcasting Act. Section 10 reads as follows-
Mr. Speaker-
-and it is related to section 17 which we are considering now-before my hon. friend raises unnecessarily a point of order-
I just wanted to ask the hon. member whether he would allow me to ask him a question.
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Is the
hon. gentleman rising on a question of privilege?
No.
I am merely asking the permission to put a question to the hon. member.
By all means.
Does the hon. member think it is worse to criticize confederation than to criticize the Queen?

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that we are engaging on a fairly controversial subject, and I know of no hon. member sitting in the House of Commons presently who has ever criticized in any way a reigning monarch. I do not know a single case when that happened. Perhaps the hon. member is referring to certain statements of principle I made and I do not regret. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I have always advocated that Canada must be truly Canadian and have truly distinctive symbols. I would ask, for instance, the hon. member if he agrees with me when I set forth principles that are not

an attack against the reigning sovereign and a lawfully constituted authority.
Mr. Speaker, I now come to section 10 of the act-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order.
I shall have to ask the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) to discuss the principle of the bill before us.

Mr. Speaker, I readily submit to your ruling in discussing the bill under consideration. Its purpose is to amend a clause concerning programs of a political nature. We agree, Mr. Speaker, with the amendment as stated; that amendment is so clear and so interesting that we are naturally inclined to relate this principle to another one which is just as important.
So that clause 17 is well understood, I should like to read section 10 of the Broadcasting Act, which is as follows:
The board shall, for the purpose of ensuring the continued existence and efficient operation of a national broadcasting system and the provision of a varied and comprehensive broadcasting service of a high standard that is basically Canadian in content and character, regulate the establishment and operation of networks of broadcasting stations, the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them and provide for the final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto.
Mr. Speaker, that section cannot be clearer and when television stations allow political speeches aimed at destroying the federal system as such, when political programs of a partisan nature endeavour to disrupt the federal system as it is, I say that those programs are basically illegal and that section 15 as well as section. 18 of the Broadcasting Act should apply in order to prohibit such programs.
That is why I commend the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley) who made a point of clarifing the situation concerning political broadcasts.
I hope that, when his bill is referred to the committee on privileges and elections, the Broadcasting Act will be fully reviewed, so as to allow the board of broadcast governors to exercise its prerogatives, powers and duties, as set out therein.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Halton and I just had those few remarks to make.

I agree there is a desperate need for some amendment to the regulations respecting political
Broadcasting Act
broadcasting during political campaigns, and particularly before election dates, which is the main matter dealt with in this bill. I am not sure what the interpretation of one of the clauses should be-whether or not there are to be two consecutive days preceding the election or whether there will be one day ahead of the election date. It is not completely clear and perhaps it can be clarified.
This matter of public relations and the persuasion of the public by political parties is very difficult to control. It is also, in my opinion, a most difficult task to write a set of regulations which would have the effect of providing equal opportunity for the various political parties so as not to give one of them an advantage over the others. This is true, I think, notwithstanding the size of the various parties, if we consider that size on the basis of representation in the House of Commons is the criterion. We know, for example, that we cannot even buy national network time from the C.B.C. for political broadcasting. Some time is made available, but it is granted as free time. I do not intend to argue now whether this is an advantage or not, but I certainly do have a grievance about the way in which this time is apportioned. For example, at federal level the corporation imposes a number of conditions which a political party must meet before it gets any time at all. Yet we know that they violate more than 50 per cent of those conditions in the apportionment of the free time. Even worse, they do not use the same formula when it comes to granting free time in connection with provincial elections. I know that in Alberta during the years 1959 to 1963 there were 61 Social Credit members of the legislature and one Conservative. During all that time the Conservatives got equal time; the Conservative party had just as much time as the Social Credit party, in spite of the fact that the proportion of representation in the house was 61 to 1. There were times when the New Democratic party, for example, were granted equal time, and they did not have any members. I am not exactly sure what the case is now, but I think the Conservatives are still getting free time on provincial affairs broadcasts, and they do not have any members in either the Alberta house or the British Columbia house.
This may be a proper way to do it. I think the practice in the province of Alberta and the province of British Columbia, where they give this free time on provincial affairs broadcasts to all the four political parties who have

Broadcasting Act
run nearly a full slate of candidates, and so on, is the right one; but I say the same formula should be applied to the federal arena. During the years 1958 to 1962, when we did not have any representation in this House of Commons, they did not give us any time at all. So some major overhauling needs to be done with regard to the regulations governing the apportionment of time.
I really cannot see much point in having regulations at all if you are not going to follow them. Some of the regulations we have now demand, for example, that you run candidates in at least three provinces before getting time on national broadcasts. They say that you must contest more than 50 per cent of the seats in Canada-in other words, 133-and there are a number of other conditions. We know that the way in which this time is apportioned today is such that they do not even follow the formula set down, and therefore it is time there was a major overhaul of the whole situation regarding broadcasting time.
Getting back to one of the other points raised by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley) when he introduced this bill, I would refer to the matter of trying to equalize to some degree the opportunity for advertising between the press and the other media of public communication and information. I know that to suggest to the press that they should not accept any advertisements from political parties on the day before the election, or even on election day, would cause them immediately to scream about the freedom of the press. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, the press includes television and radio, in the present context of their function in our social order. So if we are going to insist that the radio stations and the television stations are prevented from carrying partisan political broadcasts during a specified period before election day, this should apply to the printed press as well. I am one of those who believes that the influence television and radio have on the general public, or the electorate, today is equal to or perhaps even greater than that of the printed page; therefore I see no logic at all in separating one from the other. Perhaps a case can be made out for allowing television and radio stations to continue partisan political broadcasting right up to the day before election day, but I am not arguing that at the moment; I am arguing that as far as I am concerned these three mediums cannot and should not be divided.

As far as some of the other provisions of the bill are concerned, the matter of prohibiting political broadcasts in one part of the country that is far removed from where the election is taking place is, to my mind, a silly rule. I wholeheartedly agree with the provision here to the effect that it would only need to be prohibited in the actual area where the election was taking place. That certainly seems to me a sensible thing to do. In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize that there are a great many other difficulties and anomalies in the present regulations as they apply to partisan political broadcasting, and I think this whole matter should be reviewed by a committee of the House of Commons. We should either come up with something that is reasonable and equitable to all parties and to the mediums involved, or withdraw all the regulations and allow the television stations and the radio stations to do exactly what the newspapers are doing.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would seem that most hon. members who have spoken thus far have been in complete accord with the terms of the bill as presented to us. As a matter of fact, if I thought for one moment that Your Honour would allow a discourse this afternoon that was irrelevant, such as was the case with a previous speaker, there are a few things I would like to say with regard to other debates this week; but of course I know Your Honour would not allow this. With regard to the bill before us, I think it has some good aspects and there are good and sufficient reasons for us to consider it closely to see whether there is not also a bad feature in regard to the practice thus far. I agree with the limitation contained in the amending clause 17(l)(b)(ii). I think this is a proper limitation to place on the provisions of the present act. On the other hand, in the explanatory notes for clause 1 it is stated:
The revised clause continues this prohibition-
I do not think this is quite right and I would like to say that so far as the bad features of the amendments in the bill are concerned, it is my belief-and I know this is just a part of the thinking in the amendment-that when we are concerned with a general election, by the time the public have absorbed all they have listened to or watched or read, they have had enough by the Friday night prior to an election. I am one of those who believe that the extension of the extra day is indeed not necessary.

Let us look at what might happen. I do not suggest tor one minute that any citizen of Canada who offers himself as a candidate for election would follow a course which would not be acceptable in the public eye, but if we were to accept such an amendment and continue broadcasting, particularly by television, on through the Saturday evening prior to an election, you would reach a situation where a candidate might well make some statement against his opponent which could not in any other way be refuted or dealt with, so far as the public was concerned, either by the press or by public meeting, because immediately we would run into the restriction in respect to the following Sunday and Monday. Then you would have a situation where a candidate could possibly take advantage of his opponent or opponents, and as I said before without any recourse being given the other candidate or candidates in the field.
There is some merit in all the other things which have been said, but in regard to the amendments which are before us I say again that I believe it has been the practice in these particular fields of communication to deal with the situation judiciously so that an embarrassing or hypothetical situation such as has been mentioned here several times does not occur. If it does occur and the two areas are far enough apart, then the broadcasting corporation itself would take care of the matter in the best way possible for the two areas concerned without causing a breach of the rules, and yet seeing that justice is done so far as the candidates are concerned. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, regrettably 1 would be one of those who suggests that another thought be given to the amendments before any action is taken with regard to sending this matter to the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I was greatly interested in the comments of the previous speakers, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley), the sponsor of the bill, as well as the member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe), without forgetting, of course the humorous but very pertinent remarks of my good friend, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) in connection with Bill No. C-25 under study this afternoon.
The purposes of the bill have been clearly explained by the sponsor himself and are set forth in the explanatory notes of the bill. It is more especially a question of amending a single subsection, that is subsection 1 of section 17 of the Broadcasting Act.
Broadcasting Act
Under paragraph (b) of subsection (1), no radio or television station is allowed to broadcast a political program on any of the two consecutive days before a federal, provincial or municipal election.
As it was pointed out a while ago, that provision gives rise to some rather unusual situations. Indeed, it means that if there was a municipal election in Vancouver, for instance, it would be illegal to broadcast political programs in other parts of the country during the three days preceding voting day. In the case of a provincial election in New Brunswick or of a municipal election in the west, the radio and television stations of the province concerned would not be allowed to broadcast political programs.
Of course, that is but an example, since there is no question of a provincial election in New Brunswick, for everybody knows we have there at present an excellent government.
Coming back to section 17 of Bill No. C-25, I hold that this legislation, as drafted, is ridiculous and should be amended, but I should first of all point out that the amendment itself, as proposed by the hon. member for Halton, could be somewhat amended were it referred to a committee, for we see, for instance, that the amendment, as proposed, is as follows and I quote section 17 (lXbXii):
(ii) intended to be received by the public within the electoral district either directly or through the medium of relay stations.
Mr. Speaker, I contend that the term "electoral district", even if those two words give a very good definition of a federal or provincial riding, could not be a proper definition of a municipal division, at the municipal level, where we have wards or subdivisions rather than electoral districts.
Now, the explanatory notes of the bill refer us to page 4117 of Hansard, volume 4, 1958, where we see that the then minister of national revenue proposed to refer that matter to a committee of the house. I fully agree with the then minister and with the hon. member for Halton.
Of course, when we speak of a committee with that in mind, it would be, in this case, the committee on privileges and elections. This committee, recently formed for the duration of the session, will, no doubt, consider fairly soon the Canada Elections Act. Members of the committee will, therefore, have the opportunity of considering the problem and finding a solution in conformity

Broadcasting Act
with the Canada Elections Act and the Broadcasting Act, and in accordance with the facts.
Subsection 1 of section 99 of the Canada Elections Act reads as follows:
No person shall be allowed to broadcast a speech or any entertainment or advertising program over the radio, on the ordinary polling day and on the two days immediately preceding it, in favour or on behalf of any political party or any candidate at an election.
Mr. Speaker, I must point out that paragraph 1 of section 99 of the Canada Elections Act does not stipulate any penalty. On the other hand, paragraph 2 of the same section deals with broadcasts coming from outside the country.
For instance, if candidates in federal elections in Canada go to the state of Maine and use the local television stations to broadcast political programs to Canada during an election campaign, they commit an illegal act, although there was a time when, during an election campaign, a candidate was allowed to cross over to the United States and use the services of American radio and television stations to explain, from outside Canada his political principles to a Canadian audience.
Mr. Speaker, subsection 2 of section 99 of the Canada Elections Act, as opposed to subsection 1, provides a penalty, whereas section 18 of the Broadcasting Act stipulates that:
Every person who violates any of the provisions of this part or the regulations is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction as provided in the Criminal Code.
This means that we have two acts which completely contradict one another, since the penalty clause in the Broadcasting Act refers to the Criminal Code, while the penalty clause in the Canada Elections Act provides its own penalty.
Therefore, this is a second or third discrepancy which should be studied and rectified by suggesting to the committee on privileges and elections that the appropriate and necessary amendments be made.
Mr. Speaker, if I may make a few remarks, I should like to point out that this is not the only section of the Broadcasting Act which should be revised. Many others should be looked into, as mentioned by hon. members who spoke before me.
On the other hand, how is it that radio and television stations can boost the price of their programs during an election campaign?
How is it that we read in the press and hear on the radio that politicians, regardless of political affiliations, spend too much money on election campaigns? But we seldom read
[Mr. Dub6.1
an article in the newspapers or hear commentaries over the radio or television blaming those who are actually making electoral campaigns more and more costly. I believe that we should adopt legislation or promulgate regulations establishing maximum costs so as to prevent radio or television station owners from taking advantage of elections which have come up frequently these last few years, by raising their prices and thus increasing their profits at the expense of those who wish to carve out a career for themselves in politics or become members of the federal or provincial parliament in order to serve the public.
Mr. Speaker, before closing my remarks, I wish to point out that a way of settling this last problem would be to allow free periods of time for radio or television broadcasts during election campaigns. Of course, these free periods should be limited, but equally apportioned between all legitimate candidates running in an election, in order that every one of them might have the same opportunity to express their views and make themselves heard, without having to be millionaires for that.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I move:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections for further study.

Mr. Speaker, I am only going to take about two minutes so there will be plenty of opportunity to vote on this motion. I want to make three points, and because of the lack of time they will necessarily be disjointed. First may I suggest that the time within which election broadcasting is carried on should be limited because of the fact that most of the people of the country now feel that election campaigns are far too long. We first confuse and stun people, and then we allow them to vote. My suggestion would be that a total period of 30 days terminating just before the election should be established as the time within which broadcasting may take place.
Second, I suggest that the question of dramatized form is innocuous. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette), who spoke in this debate, when in full exercise of his oratorical powers could very well be accused of making a dramatized election speech. I say this in the most kindly way, of course, but this indicates the inadvisability of including this particular provision. Are we to allow people to vote, and then say to them

that the insidious propaganda of a dramatized political program is going to deprive them of the ability to exercise their right to vote in a free and independent way? I think this is nonsense.
Finally I make the suggestion that surely we should not presume to legislate on behalf of the provinces. We should make provision that the part of the section prohibiting these broadcasts in respect of provincial legislatures or municipal corporations will apply only when the provincial legislature has seen fit to adopt and ratify it. There may be provinces who feel that their citizens are made of hardier stuff than those in other parts of Canada and who might be prepared to allow their people to be subjected to propaganda on the radio and television media. With these changes I suggest that the hon. member has done a service in bringing this matter to our attention, but we should have regard to more than what is included in the bill.
Motion (Mr. MacNaught) agreed to.
